policies.title: Subcontracted Agencies and Contract Caregivers
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Director of Nursing/Supervising RN, scheduling and human resources staff, and any independent contractor, contractual employee or subcontracted agency providing services for [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure that every individual who provides care for [AGENCY NAME] clients, whether an employee, independent contractor, contractual employee or staff of a subcontracted agency, meets the same screening and qualification requirements, and that clients are told in writing about any subcontracting.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] applies the same pre-referral screening, licensure or certification verification, health screening, training and skills assessment requirements to independent contractors and contractual employees as it does to employees. If the agency subcontracts with another licensed agency, that agency must verify the required personnel information and give [AGENCY NAME] evidence that the verification was done. Before the first visit, clients are told in writing about any subcontractual relationship with an individual or agency who will be assigned to them. Under CFC and CPAS, the agency itself employs the registered nurse; nursing oversight is not subcontracted. The classification of each caregiver (employee or independent contractor) is consistent with the Health-General §19-4A-11 worker classification certification.

definitions.definition: An individual who provides services under a written contract and is not an employee, subject to the worker classification requirements the agency has certified.
An individual who provides services for the agency under a contractual arrangement, including through another entity, and who must meet the same screening requirements as an employee.
Another licensed agency with which [AGENCY NAME] contracts to provide caregivers or services to its clients.
Documents from the subcontracted agency, such as signed attestations and copies of the records or a verification summary, showing each screening element was completed for each individual.

procedures: The Administrator approves in writing every use of an independent contractor or subcontracted agency before any individual is assigned to a client. The approval records the reason, the clients or services involved and the start date.

Before contracting with another agency, the Administrator verifies that the agency holds a current OHCQ Residential Service Agency license (or other required licensure) and, for Medicaid services, is enrolled and in good standing. A copy of the license verification is saved in the contract file.

Every subcontract is in writing. It requires the subcontracted agency to follow the same screening and training standards as this agency, to verify personnel information for each individual it assigns, to give [AGENCY NAME] evidence of that verification, to cooperate with inspections and audits, to protect client confidentiality, and to report incidents and complaints to [AGENCY NAME] immediately. It also gives [AGENCY NAME] the right to end assignments.

For an independent contractor or contractual employee, human resources completes the full pre-referral screening before the first assignment: criminal history check under Health-General Title 19, Subtitle 19; licensure or certification verification; basic health screening including TB; references; employment history; Form I-9 and identity and employment eligibility; an in-person interview; and a skills assessment and demonstration (see PER-01 through PER-04).

For individuals supplied by a subcontracted agency, human resources collects the evidence of verification for every item in step 4 before the individual is assigned. If the evidence is missing or incomplete, the individual is not assigned.

Contractor training records are kept in the personnel or contractor file. Screening records are kept in the agency's business office. Contractors complete the same required training, including personal care, recognizing situations needing RN referral, record keeping, ethics and confidentiality, CPR, standard precautions and abuse and neglect prevention (see PER-03).

The Supervising RN assigns certified or non-certified caregivers to clients by applying SVC-05, regardless of whether the caregiver is an employee or contractor. A certified caregiver is assigned when the client needs one for ADLs or for medication administration.

The Supervising RN's supervision, assessment, plan of care updates and supervisory visits apply to contractor and subcontracted caregivers just as they do to employees. The agency employs the RN for CFC and CPAS clients and does not delegate this role to a subcontractor.

Before the first visit, the intake coordinator gives each affected client or representative a written disclosure naming the individual or agency who will provide services, the nature of the subcontractual relationship, and the caregiver's name. The client or representative signs to acknowledge receipt, and the signed disclosure is placed in the client record (see CR-06).

The Administrator confirms that each caregiver's classification (employee or independent contractor) is consistent with the agency's worker classification certification under Health-General §19-4A-11 and with wage and hour rules. Questions are resolved before assignment (see PER-06 and PER-08).

The Administrator reviews each contractor and subcontracted agency at least annually: license status, evidence of verification, complaints, incidents, quality of care, and timely documentation. The results are recorded and reported to the Quality Assurance program (GOV-04).

Any caregiver conduct that may be grounds for Board of Nursing action, including conduct by a contractor or subcontracted staff, is reported immediately to the Board of Nursing and OHCQ (see PER-10). Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported under SAF-01.

If a subcontracted agency fails to give verification evidence or fails to meet a requirement, the Administrator stops new assignments, arranges replacement caregivers so clients do not lose service, notifies affected clients, and documents the corrective action or termination of the contract.

Approves each contract and subcontract, verifies licensure, monitors performance, and ensures worker classification is consistent.
Completes or collects evidence of all screening elements before assignment and files records correctly.
Employed by the agency. Assesses clients, assigns qualified caregivers and supervises contract caregivers to the same standard as employees.

policies.title: Client Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] staff, contractors and caregivers; all clients and their representatives.
policies.purpose: To make sure every client knows and can exercise his or her rights, understands his or her responsibilities, and can obtain information about how to reach the agency, the caregiver, the supervisor, OHCQ and Adult or Child Protective Services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written Client Rights and Responsibilities policy and gives it to every client or representative before services begin. Clients have the right to dignity and individuality; adequate and appropriate care; participation in planning their care; refusing treatment after the consequences are explained; privacy; freedom from mental, verbal, sexual and physical abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation; and confidentiality. Clients may complain to the agency, to government agencies or to others without threat or fear of retaliation and will receive a prompt response. Clients may accept or reject any referred caregiver without retaliation. The agency provides its 24-hour, 7-day telephone number, the caregiver's name, and the supervisor's name and contact information. The agency ensures its home and community-based services settings respect participant choice and rights consistent with federal home and community-based services requirements.

definitions.definition: An individual receiving services from [AGENCY NAME], including a Medicaid participant in CFC or CPAS.
A person legally authorized or designated by the client to act or receive information on the client's behalf.
Separating a client from others against the client's will or confining the client to a room or area.
Any adverse action, threat or change in service, schedule or treatment because a client or representative asserted a right, complained or declined a caregiver.

procedures: The intake coordinator gives the written Client Rights and Responsibilities policy to the client or representative before the first service visit. The document is in plain language and in the client's preferred language or format, with interpretation as needed (see CR-05).

The intake coordinator or Supervising RN reviews the rights and responsibilities verbally, answers questions, and confirms understanding. The client or representative signs and dates an acknowledgment, which is placed in the client record. If the client or representative declines to sign, staff note that and the reason.

The written information lists: dignity and individuality; adequate and appropriate care; participation in care planning; refusing treatment after consequences are explained; privacy; freedom from mental, verbal, sexual and physical abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation; and confidentiality.

The written information explains that clients may complain to the agency, to government agencies or to others without threat or fear of retaliation, and that the agency will respond promptly (see CR-02).

The written information includes the procedure for complaining to the Office of Health Care Quality at 800-492-6005, and to Adult Protective Services at the local department of social services (or Child Protective Services if the client is a minor). The local department contact for the client's county is written in the packet.

Before services begin, the client receives the agency's 24-hour, 7-day telephone number ([PHONE]), the assigned caregiver's name, and the name and contact information of the supervising nurse or care supervisor. Whenever the caregiver or supervisor changes, the client is given the new name before the next visit.

The client also receives the cost information required under CR-06, advance directive information under CR-08, informed consent information under CR-07, and the right to accept or reject any referred caregiver under CR-09. Rights are also explained when the client's service plan changes substantially.
Caregivers receive training on client rights at orientation and annually (PER-03). They are told that they must honor client choices, protect privacy, and never retaliate against a client.

Staff honor a client's refusal of treatment or service after the Supervising RN explains the consequences. The refusal is documented in the client record, the plan of care is updated as appropriate, and the client's physician or supports planner is told as required (see SVC-03 and SVC-13).

The agency does not suspend, discontinue or change a client's services because the client exercised a right, filed a complaint, or declined a caregiver. Any proposed change in services follows SVC-12.

Any staff member who suspects a violation of client rights, including abuse, neglect, exploitation or retaliation, reports it immediately to the Administrator. Abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported under SAF-01 and the agency's complaint process under CR-02 is followed.

The Administrator reviews rights-related complaints and incidents at least quarterly with the quality assurance committee and updates this policy, forms and training as needed. The client rights policy is reviewed at least annually under GOV-03.
The agency keeps a copy of the current rights policy available at the office and gives another copy to any client who asks.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the rights policy is current, available and enforced, and that no retaliation occurs.
Reviews rights during assessment and supervisory visits, explains consequences of refusing treatment, and documents client choices.
Provides the written policy, phone numbers, caregiver and supervisor names, and obtains the signed acknowledgment.
Treat clients with dignity, respect privacy and choices, and report any rights concern immediately.

documentation: Current written Client Rights and Responsibilities policy
Signed acknowledgment of receipt for each client
Record of caregiver, supervisor and 24/7 number given to client
Documentation of refusals of treatment and explanation of consequences
Client rights training records

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] staff, contractors and caregivers; clients, representatives and families.
policies.purpose: To give clients and others a clear process to raise complaints, to make sure complaints are investigated and answered promptly without disrupting services or causing retaliation, and to meet reporting requirements to OHCQ and the Department of Health.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains an internal complaint process. Clients are told about it and about the OHCQ complaint hotline (800-492-6005) when services begin. Written complaints are investigated in a timely way, and services are not disrupted because a complaint was filed. Each investigation report records the time, date, place and individuals involved, a complete description of the complaint, the disposition and follow-up steps to prevent recurrence. If no investigation is done, the reason is documented in the complaint record. The agency notifies the client or representative, the physician if needed, and licensing or law enforcement agencies when required. For Medicaid participants, complaints are reported within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge, with a written report within 7 calendar days on the Department's form. Reports are given to OHCQ immediately on request, and a public summary is available on request as permitted by law.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction or concern about the agency's services, staff, billing or conduct, whether oral or written and whether from a client, representative, family member, staff or other person.
The written record of the agency's review of a complaint, including time, date, place, individuals involved, full description, disposition and follow-up.
The person designated by the Administrator to receive, log and manage complaints ([NAME/TITLE]).
The outcome of the investigation, such as substantiated, unsubstantiated, or resolved, with the action taken.

procedures: At admission, the intake coordinator explains the complaint process to the client or representative and gives written information that includes how to complain to the agency ([PHONE]) and the OHCQ hotline number (800-492-6005). Adult Protective Services contact information is given as described in CR-01.

Any staff member who receives a complaint, oral or written, records the date, time, complainant and substance, and gives it to the complaint coordinator the same business day. Staff must not discourage, delay or retaliate against anyone who wants to complain.

The complaint coordinator logs the complaint with a unique number and notifies the Administrator the same business day. Complaints that allege abuse, neglect, exploitation, injury or a threat to safety are handled immediately under SAF-01 and SAF-02, and protective steps are taken first.

The complaint coordinator acknowledges receipt to the complainant within 2 business days. The agency's internal target is to complete the investigation and respond in writing within 14 calendar days, and the complainant is informed if more time is needed and why.

For a Medicaid participant, the Administrator reports the complaint within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge to the Department as required and submits the written report within 7 calendar days of knowledge on the Department's form. The date, time and method of each report are logged.

The complaint coordinator, or an appropriate person who is not involved in the complaint, investigates. The investigator interviews the complainant, client, caregivers and witnesses as relevant, reviews records such as visit records, the plan of care and schedules, and visits the home if needed.

The investigation report records the time, date and place of the events, the individuals involved, a full description of the complaint and findings, the disposition, and the follow-up steps to prevent recurrence, with names and dates for each step. The Administrator reviews and signs the report.

If the agency decides not to investigate, for example because the complaint is withdrawn or duplicates one already investigated, the complaint coordinator documents the specific reason in the complaint record and the Administrator approves it.

Services to the client continue without interruption during the complaint process. If the complaint concerns a caregiver, the Supervising RN arranges a different qualified caregiver, if the client asks or safety requires, without penalizing the client (see CR-09).

The Administrator notifies the client or representative of the result in writing. As needed, the agency also notifies the client's physician, supports planner or case manager, and any licensing agency or law enforcement agency. Notifications are documented with date, person and method.
The agency never retaliates against a complainant, and staff who retaliate are subject to discipline up to and including termination (PER-07).

Complaint investigation reports are sent to OHCQ immediately on request. A summary of complaints, without identifying information, is made available to the public on request as permitted by law, and the Administrator reviews it first for confidentiality (CR-03).

The Administrator reviews complaint trends at least quarterly with the Quality Assurance program (GOV-04), decides on corrective action such as retraining, schedule changes or discipline, and documents the action.
Complaint records are kept with the agency's administrative records and the relevant client record in accordance with REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Is accountable for the complaint process, makes the 24-hour and 7-day Medicaid reports, approves reports and ensures no retaliation.
Logs, acknowledges, investigates or assigns, and tracks every complaint to completion.
Contributes clinical review, arranges caregiver changes and ensures continuity of services.
Accept complaints, forward them the same business day, and cooperate with investigations.

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] employees, contractors, subcontracted staff, volunteers and business associates who may see or hear client information.
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and confidentiality of client information in every form, to release information only as allowed, and to respond correctly to any suspected improper use or disclosure.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps client records and information confidential. Medical information is released only with the written consent of the client or representative, or as permitted by Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3. Records are protected by safeguards against loss, destruction, and illegal or unauthorized use. All staff are trained in ethical behavior and confidentiality. The agency documents the client's representative who has authority to receive information. The agency applies the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164), including the minimum necessary standard, and protects client information on paper, in electronic systems and on devices.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health information about a client, in any form, that the agency creates, receives or keeps.
The standard that staff use, disclose or request only the amount of PHI needed to do the task.
An unauthorized acquisition, access, use or disclosure of PHI that compromises its privacy or security, unless a risk assessment shows a low probability that the PHI was compromised.
The person designated by the Administrator to manage privacy practices, complaints and breach response ([NAME/TITLE]).
A person documented in the client record as having authority to act or receive information for the client.

procedures: The Administrator designates a Privacy Officer and a Security Officer (who may be the same person) in writing. Their names are listed in the staff manual.

At admission, the intake coordinator gives the client or representative the Notice of Privacy Practices and asks for a signed acknowledgment, which goes in the client record. The intake coordinator also records who the client's representative is, with documentation of the authority, and what information that person may receive.

Staff may use or disclose client information for treatment, payment and agency operations as permitted by HIPAA. All other disclosures require a written authorization signed by the client or representative, unless Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3 or other law permits the release. The Privacy Officer approves non-routine releases and records them in a disclosure log.

Staff access only the PHI needed for their job duties. Caregivers receive only the information needed for safe care. Supervisors and billing staff are given role-based access in the electronic system, and the Administrator reviews access quarterly.

Caregivers do not discuss clients or share information about them in public places, with other clients, on social media, or with anyone not involved in care. They do not photograph or record clients without written consent.

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets in the business office, and client information in the home is limited to what is needed. Records are never left in vehicles or in view of others. Electronic systems require unique user IDs, strong passwords, automatic log-off and encryption. Staff may use personal devices for client information only if they follow the device security rules in the Security Officer's written procedure.

Text messages, email and the telephonic ISAS system are used only for the minimum information needed. Texts and emails containing PHI are sent only through secure methods approved by the Security Officer.

All staff are trained on ethical behavior and confidentiality at orientation, before they have contact with client information, and annually (PER-03). Each person signs a confidentiality agreement, which is kept in the personnel file (PER-05).

Client records are protected against loss, destruction and unauthorized use through locked storage, access controls, regular backups and a written disaster recovery procedure. Records are kept and destroyed under REC-01, and are completed within 30 days of a client's discharge.

A client or representative may ask to inspect or receive a copy of the record, request an amendment, ask for an accounting of disclosures or ask for restrictions. The Privacy Officer responds in writing within the time required by HIPAA, generally within 30 days, and documents the response.
Staff must report any suspected privacy incident, such as a lost device, misdirected fax or email, or snooping, to the Privacy Officer immediately and no later than the same business day.

The Privacy Officer investigates and completes a documented risk assessment of the nature of the PHI, the person who received it, whether it was actually viewed, and how far the risk was reduced. If a breach is found, the agency notifies affected clients without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery, and makes the other notifications to the Department of Health and Human Services and, if required, the media, as HIPAA requires.

The agency has a written agreement with every business associate, such as an electronic record vendor or billing service, that handles PHI. The Privacy Officer reviews those agreements annually. Subcontracted agencies and contractors are bound to the same confidentiality duties (GOV-09).

Violations of this policy are subject to discipline up to termination (PER-07), and no one is retaliated against for reporting a privacy concern. The Privacy Officer reviews privacy incidents and training at least annually and reports to the Governing Authority.

responsibilities.duty: Is accountable for privacy compliance, designates the Privacy and Security Officers and ensures resources and discipline.
Approves releases, handles client requests and complaints, assesses and responds to breaches, and keeps the disclosure log.
Manages access controls, device and electronic security, backups and secure communication methods.
Provides the Notice of Privacy Practices, records the representative and obtains authorizations.
Protect client information, use the minimum necessary, complete training and report incidents immediately.

documentation: Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments
Documentation of client representative and the information they may receive
Signed authorizations and disclosure log
Staff confidentiality agreements and training records
Access and security reviews
Privacy incident and breach risk assessments and notifications
Business associate agreements
Records of client requests for access, amendment or accounting

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All employees, independent contractors and contractual employees of [AGENCY NAME], including the Administrator, RN Supervisor, office staff and caregivers, for all clients regardless of payer
policies.purpose: To protect clients' property and money and to prevent financial exploitation. To keep staff free of conflicts of interest with the clients they serve. To make sure any suspected exploitation is reported promptly to the right authorities.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] protects every client's right to be free from abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation. Staff will not borrow from, accept gifts from, or take any financial advantage of a client or the client's family. Staff will not be named as a beneficiary in a client's will, or act as a client's agent under a power of attorney, unless a family relationship exists and the Administrator has reviewed it. Staff will not hold or manage a client's funds, accounts, cards, checks or passwords. The only exception is a documented errand that is in the plan of care or is specifically authorized in writing by the client or representative, with receipts. Any suspected exploitation of a client is reported immediately to the local department of social services. For Medicaid participants it is also reported to the Department within 24 hours of knowledge, with a written report within 7 calendar days. The agency will remain free of conflicts of interest as a Medicaid provider. Retaliation against anyone who reports a concern is prohibited.

definitions.definition: Improper use of a client's money, property, benefits or credit for the benefit of someone other than the client. This includes theft, forgery, coercion, undue influence, borrowing without repayment, and accepting gifts or inheritance obtained through pressure or a position of trust.
A purchase or task done outside the home for the client (for example groceries or a pharmacy pickup) that is listed in the plan of care or authorized in writing by the client or representative.

A personal, financial or family interest of staff or the agency that could influence, or appear to influence, care decisions or billing. Examples include a financial relationship with a client or influencing a client's choice of provider for personal gain.
A beverage or snack offered by a client and consumed during a visit. It is not a gift under this policy.

procedures: At hire and before first client contact, the Administrator gives each staff member a written copy of this policy. The staff member signs an acknowledgment that is filed in the personnel record.

Orientation training on abuse, neglect and exploitation prevention (see SAF-01 and PER-03) includes financial exploitation. It covers warning signs such as unexplained missing money, sudden changes in accounts or wills, unpaid bills, and new people controlling finances. The training date and content are documented in the personnel file.
Caregivers must not borrow money or items from, lend money to, sell anything to, or buy anything from a client or the client's family.

Caregivers must not accept gifts, tips, loans, bequests or items of value from clients or families. Nominal hospitality is allowed. When a gift is offered, the caregiver politely declines and tells the RN Supervisor the same day. The RN Supervisor logs the offer.

Staff must not be present as a witness, or take part, in the signing of a client's will, power of attorney, deed or financial instrument. Staff must not accept appointment as agent, executor, trustee, joint account holder or beneficiary. Any exception for a documented family relationship requires prior written Administrator review.

Caregivers must not keep, use or learn a client's bank card, PIN, checks, passwords or account information. If a client asks for this kind of help, the caregiver stops and tells the RN Supervisor. The RN Supervisor reviews the request with the client and representative.
Errands require an entry in the plan of care or a signed authorization from the client or representative. The RN Supervisor reviews it before the first errand.

For each errand, the caregiver obtains the client's money in a documented amount and keeps the client's money separate from the caregiver's own. The caregiver obtains an itemized receipt and returns the receipt and exact change to the client. The caregiver and client both sign the Errand and Receipt Log at the time of return.

Caregivers do not use their own money for client purchases and do not use client funds for personal expenses or transportation costs. Mileage and any other costs are handled only as written in the service agreement (see CR-06).
Caregivers do not take client belongings out of the home except for an authorized errand item. They do not borrow client items such as phones, vehicles or tools.

When a client reports missing or damaged property, the caregiver or other staff member tells the RN Supervisor the same day. The RN Supervisor documents what was reported, checks with the client and representative, and completes an incident report under SAF-02 within 24 hours of learning of the loss.

Any staff member who suspects financial exploitation by anyone, including staff, family or others, must report it immediately by phone to the local department of social services at [LOCAL DSS PHONE] and to the Administrator at [PHONE]. If the suspected exploiter is the Administrator, the report goes to the governing authority and directly to the local department of social services.

For Medicaid participants, the Administrator reports the incident to the Department within 24 hours of knowledge and submits the written report on the Department's form within 7 calendar days. The Administrator may also contact OHCQ at 410-402-8040, or at 800-492-6005 for complaints.

The Administrator removes or reassigns any staff member under investigation so that the staff member has no unsupervised contact with the affected client. The agency preserves records and receipts, and cooperates with investigators.

Staff disclose any personal, financial or family relationship with a client, or any other possible conflict of interest, to the Administrator in writing. The Administrator reviews each disclosure and documents the outcome in the personnel file.
Any staff member who violates this policy is subject to discipline up to termination. Conduct that may be grounds for Board of Nursing action is reported under PER-10.
The Compliance Officer reviews all property-loss reports, errand logs and gift-offer logs at least quarterly and reports trends to the QA committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, reviews conflict-of-interest disclosures, makes required reports within the deadlines, and removes staff from contact with clients when exploitation is alleged.
Reviews errand authorizations, logs gift offers, follows up on property-loss reports, and discusses finance-related requests with clients and representatives.
Follows the prohibitions on gifts, loans and fund handling, keeps accurate receipts and logs, and reports suspected exploitation immediately.
Audits errand logs, gift logs and property-loss reports each quarter and reports trends to QA.
Receives and acts on any report that involves the Administrator.

documentation: Signed staff policy acknowledgment (personnel file)
Orientation and annual training record covering exploitation prevention
Errand authorization (plan of care or signed authorization) and Errand and Receipt Log with itemized receipts
Gift-offer log
Property loss and damage reports and incident reports (SAF-02)
Copies of reports to the local department of social services and the Department, with dates and times
Conflict-of-interest disclosures and Administrator determinations
Quarterly compliance review summaries

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, independent contractors and contractual employees of [AGENCY NAME] who have contact with clients, applicants, representatives or the public
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
policies.purpose: To make sure every person is treated with dignity and individuality and has equal access to services. To make sure people with limited English proficiency and people with disabilities can understand their care, their rights and how to complain.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in accepting, serving or discharging clients on the basis of race, color, national origin (including limited English proficiency), disability, age, sex, religion, or any other basis prohibited by law. The agency complies with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Clients are treated with dignity and individuality. Clients may accept or reject any referred caregiver without retaliation. The agency provides free interpreter and translation services and effective communication aids so that clients can understand and take part in their care. Written rights and complaint information is given in a form the client can understand. COMAR 10.07.05 does not set separate language access rules, so the agency follows its Title VI and ADA obligations.

definitions.definition: A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to take part in care and decisions about care.

A person who is fluent in English and the client's language, is trained in interpreting and ethics, and is competent to interpret accurately and impartially. A bilingual staff member qualifies only after the agency has assessed his or her skills.

Tools and services that make communication effective for people with disabilities, such as sign language interpreters, large-print or Braille materials, captioning, amplification, and the use of communication boards.
Communication with people with disabilities that is as effective as communication with others.

procedures: At first contact and again at intake, the Intake Coordinator asks the client and representative which language they prefer for spoken and written information. The Intake Coordinator also asks whether they need any communication aid, such as large print, sign language, hearing amplification or a communication device. The answers are recorded in the client record.

The Intake Coordinator accepts and processes referrals without regard to the client's race, color, national origin, disability, age, sex, religion or other protected status. Reasons for declining a referral are limited to documented service capacity, staffing or the inability to safely meet needs under SVC-02. The Administrator reviews and signs every referral decline.

The Administrator keeps a list of interpreter resources, such as a telephone or video interpreting vendor, qualified community interpreters and bilingual staff who have been assessed. The list is available to all staff and is reviewed every year.

Whenever a client with LEP needs to understand information, the staff member uses a qualified interpreter. This includes intake, consent, rights, care planning and plan changes, supervisory visits and grievances. [AGENCY NAME] pays for the interpreter and the client is never charged.

Staff do not require or ask clients to bring their own interpreter. Staff may use a family member or friend only if the client freely chooses this after being told that a free qualified interpreter is available. This choice is documented. Minor children are never used as interpreters except in a life-threatening emergency when no other interpreter is available.

The RN Supervisor or Intake Coordinator gives the client's written rights, complaint procedures (including the OHCQ and local department of social services complaint information), cost estimate and plan of care in the client's preferred language. If translated documents are not available, a qualified interpreter reads or sight-translates them. The staff member documents who interpreted, the language and the date.

The Administrator has the agency's key client documents (client rights, grievance procedure, service agreement, consent and waiver forms, and emergency instructions) translated into the languages most frequently needed in the agency's service area. The Administrator reviews the languages needed each year using intake data.

For clients with disabilities, the RN Supervisor identifies communication needs at the assessment and lists them in the plan of care. Staff provide the necessary auxiliary aids at no cost to the client. Examples include reading documents aloud, large-print copies, written communication, sign language interpreters, and extra time.

Caregivers are told of each client's communication needs and language before the first visit. Caregivers must not use other people's phone numbers, or assumptions about a client's understanding, in place of an interpreter. They report communication barriers to the RN Supervisor.

Staff do not make assumptions about a client's abilities, preferences or care needs based on disability, age, race, national origin or language. Caregivers address clients by their preferred name and respect their cultural, religious and personal practices as far as they are consistent with safe care.

Clients may accept or reject any referred caregiver without retaliation (see CR-09). The agency does not reduce, delay or change the services of any client who asks for a different caregiver, makes a complaint, or uses an interpreter.

No staff member may use slurs or demeaning language, harass a client or coworker, or refuse to serve a client because of a protected characteristic. Concerns are reported to the Administrator and handled under CR-02 and PER-07. Substantiated violations lead to discipline up to termination.

The Administrator posts a nondiscrimination statement, in English and the other main languages of the service area, in the office and on the agency's website if there is one. The statement tells people how to ask for an interpreter or aid and how to file a complaint with the agency, with OHCQ at 800-492-6005, and with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights.
Orientation and annual training (see PER-03) cover this policy, how to work with interpreters, and how to communicate with clients who have disabilities. Training is documented in the personnel file.

The Compliance Officer reviews the interpreter log, complaints and referral decline records every quarter. The review checks for unequal access or treatment. Findings go to the QA committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains interpreter resources and translated materials, signs referral declines, posts the nondiscrimination notice, and ensures corrective action for violations.
Asks about language and communication needs at first contact, arranges interpreters and aids, and documents them.
Identifies communication needs at assessment, includes them in the plan of care, and ensures rights information is understood by the client.
Treats every client with dignity, uses the communication methods in the plan of care, and reports communication barriers.
Reviews interpreter logs, complaints and referral declines every quarter and reports patterns to QA.

documentation: Language and communication needs in the client record
Interpreter and translation log (date, language, interpreter, purpose)
Documentation of any client's informed choice to use a family member or friend as interpreter
Translated key documents and the list of languages
Referral decline records with reasons and Administrator signature
Posted nondiscrimination notice
Training records
Quarterly review summaries

policies.title: Service Agreement, Cost Estimates, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake and billing staff, RN Supervisor and any employee who discusses costs or services with clients or representatives; all private-pay and Medicaid clients
policies.purpose: To make sure every client or representative knows what services will cost, what they will pay, who will provide care, who to call and how they will be billed, before services start and whenever anything changes.
policies.policy: Before services start, [AGENCY NAME] gives each client or representative a written service agreement and a written estimate of the costs of the requested services. The agency also gives a statement of the costs the client is responsible for if a third-party payor will not cover the services. Itemized bills are provided on request. Clients are told the caregiver's name, the name and contact information of the care supervisor, the 24-hour, 7-day-a-week phone number, and any subcontractual relationship used to provide their care. For Medicaid clients under Community First Choice and CPAS, the agency bills only for services preauthorized in the plan of service and is paid the lesser of its usual and customary charge to the general public or the Medicaid fee schedule rate. Any change to rates or services is explained in writing in advance.

definitions.definition: The written agreement between the agency and the client or representative that describes the services, schedule, rates, billing practices, rights and responsibilities.
A written, itemized projection of the charges for the requested services, based on the expected hours or units and the applicable rates.
The rate [AGENCY NAME] charges the general public for the same service.
The rate set by the Maryland Department of Health for a Medicaid service code, published at least annually.
A 15-minute unit of personal assistance. Services up to 12 hours per day are paid in units, and a daily rate applies above 12 hours per day.

procedures: During intake, the Intake Coordinator asks how the client plans to pay (Medicaid CFC or CPAS, private pay, long-term care insurance or another source) and records it. The Intake Coordinator verifies Medicaid eligibility and authorized hours as described in SVC-02 and SVC-09.

Before the first visit, the Intake Coordinator or Administrator prepares a written cost estimate for the services requested. It lists each service, the expected frequency and hours, the rate and the estimated total for a defined period. The agency's private-pay rates are listed in the current Rate Schedule, [PRIVATE-PAY RATE SCHEDULE].

For clients who may not be covered by a third-party payor, the written estimate includes a statement of the costs the client will pay out of pocket. This includes services not covered, hours beyond those authorized, and any other charges.

For Medicaid clients, the Intake Coordinator reviews the plan of service and tells the client the number of hours and units authorized. The Intake Coordinator tells the client that Medicaid services are billed only as preauthorized and that the agency may not bill for services not in the plan of service. The agency does not charge the participant for authorized Medicaid services, except as Medicaid requirements allow.

The Administrator keeps the current Medicaid fee schedule on file and confirms it each July 1 and whenever the Department issues a new transmittal. The rates in effect at the time of adoption are $6.3962 per 15-minute unit for personal assistance (W5519 CFC; W5527 CPAS), $4.2597 per 15 minutes for shared attendant (W5521; W5528), and $329.84 per day for more than 12 hours per day (W5532). The Administrator verifies these figures against the current fee schedule before use. Rates are subject to change by the Department.

Medicaid payment is the lesser of the agency's usual and customary charge or the fee schedule rate. The Billing Manager compares the agency's charge for the general public to the fee schedule rate each year and whenever the agency's private-pay rates change. The comparison is documented.

The RN Supervisor or Intake Coordinator reviews the service agreement with the client or representative, using an interpreter if needed (see CR-05). The agreement is signed and dated by the client or representative and an agency representative. A copy is given to the client and a copy is placed in the client record.

At or before the first visit, the agency gives the client in writing: the caregiver's name; the name and contact information of the RN Supervisor or care supervisor; the 24/7 phone number, [24/7 PHONE]; and the agency's rights and complaint information (see CR-01 and CR-02).

If any part of the client's care is provided by a subcontracted agency or contract caregiver, the Intake Coordinator tells the client in writing, before services start, who the subcontractor is and what it will do (see GOV-09). The disclosure is documented in the service agreement.

The Billing Manager provides an itemized bill to any client or representative on request, within [NUMBER] business days. An itemized bill lists the date of service, hours or units, service provided, unit charge and total. Medicaid records are available according to Medicaid rules.

The Billing Manager bills private-pay clients only for services delivered and documented. Time billed matches caregiver time records (see SVC-08). Billing errors are corrected promptly and the client is notified and given a refund or credit within [NUMBER] days.
For Medicaid claims, services are billed only for time documented through the Department-approved telephonic timekeeping system (see SVC-08), within the Medicaid billing time limits (see SVC-14).

Before any change in rates, services, schedule or payment source, the RN Supervisor or Administrator gives the client or representative advance written notice and a revised cost estimate. A new signature is obtained. For Medicaid participants, services are not increased, reduced or ended without Department authorization (see SVC-12).
Clients may ask questions about charges at any time. The Billing Manager responds within [NUMBER] business days and documents the contact. Disputes are handled under CR-02.
The Billing Manager reviews all service agreements, estimates and complaints about billing every quarter and reports findings to the Compliance Officer (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the rate schedule, confirms current Medicaid rates, ensures estimates and agreements are given before services begin, and approves any changes in advance.
Prepares estimates, reviews the agreement with the client, collects signatures, and makes required disclosures including subcontractors.
Reviews services and hours with the client, explains the plan of care in relation to the estimate, and provides the supervisor contact information.
Applies the lesser-of rule, bills only documented services at the correct rate, produces itemized bills on request, and corrects errors.
Audits agreements, estimates, bills and complaints each quarter.

documentation: Signed and dated service agreement
Written cost estimate and statement of non-covered costs
Written notice of caregiver name, supervisor contact and 24/7 phone number
Subcontract disclosure
Current private-pay rate schedule and Medicaid fee schedule with date confirmed
Annual usual-and-customary versus fee schedule comparison
Itemized bills and requests for them
Advance notices of rate or service changes and revised estimates
Billing correction and refund records

policies.title: Informed Consent and Waiver of Skilled Services
policies.applies_to: RN Supervisor, Intake Coordinator, Administrator and all staff involved in obtaining consent or assigning caregivers; all clients
policies.purpose: To make sure clients make informed decisions about their care, including changes in the plan of care, routine treatments and medication self-administration by non-licensed staff. To make sure any waiver of skilled services is voluntary, informed and documented, and that only an eligible client may sign one.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] obtains informed consent before starting services and before any change in the plan of care. Consent is also obtained before non-licensed staff perform routine treatments or assist with medication self-administration. Consent follows a documented discussion of risks and benefits. The consent form is signed and dated by the client or by a representative with legal authority, and a copy is kept in the client record. Only a cognitively capable adult client, and not a representative, may sign a waiver of skilled services. The agency provides a non-certified caregiver only in the three situations allowed by COMAR 10.07.05.10D: the client needs no help with activities of daily living (ADLs); the client needs ADL help that, in the supervising nurse's judgment, has no predictable adverse health consequences; or the client signs a waiver of skilled services. The agency honors refusal of treatment and the right to withdraw consent at any time. A waiver does not replace requirements that apply to Medicaid participants or to medication administration, which requires licensed or certified staff.

definitions.definition: A client's voluntary agreement to a service or change in care after receiving information about its purpose, alternatives, side effects and benefits, cost, and the right to withdraw.

A signed statement by a cognitively capable adult client that he or she understands the risks and benefits and chooses to receive care from a non-certified caregiver, or to decline recommended skilled care.
A certified nursing assistant (CNA) or certified medication technician (CMT), or other staff who hold the certification required for the task.
A client age 18 or older who the RN has assessed as able to understand the information and the consequences of the decision and to communicate a choice.
The client takes his or her own medication, with reminders or assistance from staff as permitted by the plan of care and SVC-06.

procedures: At the initial RN assessment, the RN Supervisor reviews the client's needs and decides who may provide care. The RN determines whether the client needs ADL help, whether any predictable adverse health consequences exist if a non-certified caregiver provides that help, and whether a certified caregiver is needed (see SVC-05).

The RN Supervisor explains to the client, in plain language and with an interpreter if needed (see CR-05): the purpose and nature of the proposed treatment or service; alternatives; possible side effects and benefits; estimated costs; and the right to withdraw consent at any time.
The RN Supervisor documents the risk and benefit discussion in the client record. The note includes the date, who was present, the topics discussed, the client's questions and the client's decision.

The client or representative with legal authority signs and dates the informed consent form. The authority of a representative is verified under CR-08. The RN Supervisor signs the form as the person who explained it. A copy goes to the client and the original to the record.

Informed consent is obtained before services start, before any change in the plan of care, and before non-licensed staff perform routine treatments or assist with medication self-administration. The RN Supervisor obtains the new consent and documents the discussion when a change is proposed.

If a client is not able to give consent, the RN Supervisor identifies the legally authorized representative (see CR-08), obtains consent from that person, and still explains the care to the client in a way the client can understand.

A client who needs ADL help that may have predictable adverse health consequences if given by a non-certified caregiver is assigned a certified caregiver. The agency offers a waiver only if the client wishes to receive care from a non-certified caregiver after the RN explains the choice. The RN Supervisor does not suggest or pressure a client to waive.

Only the client may sign a waiver of skilled services, and only if the RN Supervisor has assessed that the client is a cognitively capable adult. A representative, family member, guardian or agent may not sign a waiver on the client's behalf. The RN documents the capacity assessment in the record.

Before the waiver is signed, the RN Supervisor reviews the specific skilled services or certified care being waived, the specific risks and benefits, and the alternatives, including the option of accepting a certified caregiver. The waiver form lists the services waived and the type of caregiver the client will receive.

The client signs and dates the waiver. The RN Supervisor signs and dates it. A copy is given to the client and a copy is placed in the client record. The waiver is reviewed with the client at each supervisory visit and at the annual reassessment, and whenever the client's condition changes.

A waiver does not allow staff to administer medications. Medication administration requires licensed or certified staff and physician orders (see SVC-06). For Medicaid participants, the waiver does not override Medicaid requirements for CMTs for medication administration or for CNAs and CMTs for delegated nursing functions (see SVC-05).

The client may withdraw a waiver or consent at any time, orally or in writing. The staff member who receives the withdrawal tells the RN Supervisor the same day. The RN Supervisor reassigns a certified caregiver or revises the plan of care as needed and documents the change.

If a client refuses a treatment or service, staff respect the decision. The RN Supervisor explains the possible consequences, documents the refusal, notifies the physician or other authorized person if the refusal affects safety or orders, and revises the plan of care as appropriate. Refusal does not by itself lead to discharge (see SVC-12).

If the client's condition changes, the RN Supervisor reassesses the client within the time frames of SVC-03 and SVC-10 and re-evaluates whether the waiver and the type of caregiver remain appropriate. If the client loses the capacity to make the decision, the waiver ends and the agency assigns a certified caregiver as required.
The Compliance Officer audits a sample of client records every quarter to confirm that consents and waivers are signed, dated, in the record, and match the caregiver actually assigned.

responsibilities.duty: Assesses capacity and need, explains risks and benefits, obtains and documents consent and waivers, reviews waivers regularly, and ensures the caregiver assigned matches the consent and waiver.
Provides consent forms, schedules the RN discussion and files signed forms in the record.
Ensures forms and procedures comply with this policy and that no non-certified caregiver is assigned outside the three allowed situations.
Works only within the consent and waiver on file, reports a client's withdrawal or refusal to the RN Supervisor the same day.
Audits consents and waivers every quarter.

documentation: Signed and dated informed consent forms
RN note documenting the risk and benefit discussion
Signed and dated waiver of skilled services signed by the client
RN capacity assessment
Documentation of withdrawal of consent or waiver and refusal of treatment
Waiver review notes (supervisory visits and annual reassessment)
Caregiver assignment records showing the basis for assigning a certified or non-certified caregiver
Quarterly audit results

policies.title: Client Representatives and Advance Directives
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Intake Coordinator, RN Supervisor and all staff who deal with clients' representatives or advance directive information
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] recognizes valid client representatives and only within their lawful authority. To give clients information about advance directives and use their directives to plan care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] recognizes as a client's representative a guardian of the person or property, a person named in an advance directive, a surrogate decision maker, an agent under a power of attorney, a representative payee, or a person the competent client designates in writing. The agency does not honor a representative who goes beyond the authority granted by the instrument or by State law. The agency documents the representative's name or keeps the authorizing document in the client record. Every client receives information about advance directives and the right to have one, and the agency asks for information about the client's advance directive so that it can assess the effect on care. A representative of a Medicaid participant may not be assigned as that participant's caregiver.

definitions.definition: A person legally authorized, or authorized in writing by a competent client, to act for the client within a defined scope.
A written or oral statement of a person's wishes about future health care or naming a person to make health care decisions, as recognized under Maryland law.
A person appointed by a court to make decisions for a client's person, property or both, within the scope of the court order.
A person or organization appointed by a benefits agency to manage a client's benefits, with authority limited to that purpose.

procedures: At intake, the Intake Coordinator asks each client whether he or she has a guardian, advance directive, power of attorney, surrogate decision maker, representative payee or other person designated to act on his or her behalf. The answer is recorded.

If the client is a competent adult who wants someone to act for him or her, the client designates that person in writing, in a signed and dated form that states the person's name, relationship, contact information and the decisions the person may help with. The designation is filed in the record. The client may change or cancel the designation at any time.

When a representative is named, the Intake Coordinator requests a copy of the authorizing document, such as the guardianship order, advance directive, power of attorney or payee appointment. The copy is placed in the client record. If no document is available, the representative's name and relationship are documented and the Administrator decides whether to recognize the person and records the reason.

The RN Supervisor or Administrator reads the document and records the scope of authority in the record (for example: health care decisions only, financial matters only, or limited to a specific purpose). A representative is recognized only within that scope. For example, a representative payee has no authority over care decisions, and a power of attorney for property does not authorize health care consent unless the document says so.

Staff do not honor an instruction from a person who goes beyond the authority granted by the instrument or State law. The staff member tells the RN Supervisor, who explains the limit to the person, continues to involve the client as far as the client is able, and documents the incident. The Administrator consults legal counsel when the scope of authority is unclear.
If staff believe a representative is acting against the client's interests or wishes, or is exploiting, abusing or neglecting the client, they report it immediately under SAF-01 and CR-04.

A competent client continues to make his or her own decisions. A representative named by a competent client does not replace the client's own decisions unless the client has asked for this in writing.

The RN Supervisor includes the representative's name and contact details, with the scope of authority, in the plan of care and in the information given to the caregiver. Representatives receive the client's rights, cost estimates, service agreement and notices as appropriate to their authority (see CR-01 and CR-06).

At admission, the Intake Coordinator or RN Supervisor gives each client written information about advance directives, including the client's right to make decisions about medical care, to accept or refuse treatment, and to have an advance directive. The agency does not require a client to have an advance directive, and care is not conditioned on having one.

The RN Supervisor asks whether the client has an advance directive and asks for a copy or a description. The RN assesses what effect the directive has on the services the agency provides, and documents the review in the record. A copy of the directive, if provided, is kept in the client record.

The RN Supervisor tells caregivers what they need to know about the client's advance directive, such as the location of documents and who to call, and explains that in an emergency caregivers follow SAF-02 and SVC-10 and call 911 unless the plan of care or applicable medical orders say otherwise.

If a client states a wish to create, change or cancel an advance directive, the RN Supervisor refers the client to the physician, an attorney or other appropriate resource. Agency staff do not give legal advice and do not witness, sign or help draft the document (see CR-04).

For Medicaid participants, the agency does not assign the participant's representative as that participant's caregiver. Before hiring or assigning any person, the Administrator checks whether the person is the participant's representative. If a conflict is found, the person is not assigned and the participant is told of the participant's options, and the Administrator informs the supports planner or case manager.

The RN Supervisor reviews the representative and advance directive information at each annual reassessment and whenever the client's condition changes, and updates the record. If a guardianship or authority ends or changes, the Intake Coordinator obtains a copy of the new document and updates the record.
Representative and advance directive information is kept confidential and shared only as allowed by CR-03.

responsibilities.duty: Decides on recognition when documents are unclear, obtains legal advice as needed, and prevents the assignment of a Medicaid participant's representative as the caregiver.
Asks about representatives and advance directives at intake, collects authorizing documents and gives advance directive information.
Reviews scope of authority, assesses the effect of advance directives on care, records them in the plan of care and keeps caregivers informed.
Follows instructions from recognized representatives only within their authority, and reports concerns about a representative to the RN Supervisor.

documentation: Representative's name, relationship and contact information in the record
Copy of authorizing document (guardianship order, advance directive, power of attorney, payee appointment) or the competent client's signed written designation
Record of scope of authority and any limits on recognition
Advance directive information provided to the client (date and who gave it)
RN note on the client's advance directive and its effect on care
Documentation of review at reassessment and changes in authority
Record of the check that a Medicaid participant's representative was not assigned as caregiver

policies.title: Client Choice, Participant Direction and Right to Accept or Reject Caregivers
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN Supervisor, Intake Coordinator, scheduling staff and all caregivers; Medicaid participants and clients of any payer
policies.purpose: To honor each client's right to choose a provider and caregiver and, for Medicaid participants, to direct their own personal assistance. To prevent retaliation and avoid interruptions in authorized services when a caregiver is rejected.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects client choice and participant direction. Medicaid participants have a significant role in directing their services. They may select, train, schedule, set the duties for, and dismiss the personal assistance worker in their home. Participants choose their agency during plan of service development, and the plan of service names the agency. Workers accept instruction on the required services from the participant or representative, the nurse monitor, a treating physician or nurse practitioner, or the Maryland Department of Health. Clients of any payer may accept or reject any referred caregiver without fear of retaliation. When a caregiver is rejected or dismissed, the agency arranges a replacement so that authorized services are not interrupted. These practices are consistent with the home- and community-based services requirements of 42 CFR 441.710 and 42 CFR 441.301(c) on person-centered planning, choice and participant direction.

definitions.definition: A Medicaid participant's right to direct his or her own services, including selecting, training, scheduling, setting the duties for and dismissing the worker.
The Medicaid plan that authorizes the participant's personal assistance services and names the agency the participant has chosen.
The agency RN who monitors the participant's services, assesses needs, delegates nursing tasks and supervises workers.
Any adverse action taken because a client exercised a right, such as reducing hours, delaying services, discharging the client or treating the client differently.

procedures: At intake and again at the start of services, the Intake Coordinator tells each client, orally and in writing, that the client may accept or reject any referred caregiver without fear of retaliation. For Medicaid participants, the Intake Coordinator also explains participant direction, including the right to select, train, schedule, set duties for and dismiss the worker.

For Medicaid participants, the Intake Coordinator confirms that the participant has chosen [AGENCY NAME] as the agency and that the plan of service names the agency. The Intake Coordinator confirms that the participant meets the eligibility conditions in SVC-02, including Medicaid eligibility, the level of care required for the program, and living at home. If the plan names another agency, the agency does not start services until the plan is corrected through the supports planner or case manager.

Before assigning a caregiver, scheduling staff give the client the caregiver's name and a brief description of qualifications, and ask whether the client accepts the caregiver. A participant who wants to select his or her own worker is allowed to identify the person, subject to the worker meeting all agency and Medicaid qualifications (see PER-01 and PER-02). The agency does not hire or assign anyone who does not meet them, and tells the participant the reason in writing.
The participant's representative may not be assigned as the participant's worker (see CR-08).

Participants may train their worker on how they want tasks done in their home. The RN Supervisor tells workers at orientation to the assignment that they are to follow the participant's reasonable instructions on how and when tasks are done, consistent with the plan of service and safe practice.

Participants may set the worker's schedule and duties within the authorized hours and the plan of service. Scheduling staff arrange schedules according to the participant's preferences, as far as possible. A request that would exceed authorized hours or services, or would be unsafe, is referred to the RN Supervisor, who explains the limit to the participant and, when needed, contacts the supports planner or case manager.

Workers accept instruction on the required services from the participant or representative, the nurse monitor, a treating physician or nurse practitioner, or the Department. A caregiver who gets an instruction that conflicts with the plan of service, with the law or with safe practice does not act on it and tells the RN Supervisor the same day. The RN Supervisor resolves the conflict and documents the outcome.

A client may accept or reject a referred caregiver, or ask for a different caregiver, at any time and for any reason. The client may tell any staff member. The staff member tells scheduling staff and the RN Supervisor the same day and documents the request.

A Medicaid participant may dismiss his or her worker. The participant does not have to give a reason. The RN Supervisor confirms the request with the participant, documents it, and informs the worker. The agency then follows its employment procedures for the worker without any contact with the participant that is intended to pressure the participant.

Within [NUMBER] hours of a rejection or dismissal, scheduling staff offer the client a qualified replacement. The replacement is arranged so that authorized services continue without interruption. If a same-day replacement is not possible, the RN Supervisor follows SVC-07 for continuity of care and makes sure that critical needs are met. For Medicaid participants, the RN Supervisor tells the supports planner or case manager if a gap in service cannot be avoided.

The agency does not retaliate against a client who rejects or dismisses a caregiver, makes a complaint or uses any other right. Prohibited actions include reducing or delaying services, changing the schedule without the client's agreement, threatening discharge, or treating the client differently. Services may not be suspended, terminated, increased or reduced without Department authorization and consultation with the participant (see SVC-12).
Staff do not ask clients to give a reason in writing for rejecting a caregiver, and do not ask clients to sign anything that limits this right.

A worker who tries to pressure a client to keep him or her, or retaliates against a client, is disciplined under PER-07. The Administrator reviews every report of retaliation and documents the findings.

If a client or participant says that the agency has limited his or her choice or control, the staff member records it as a grievance under CR-02. The client may also contact OHCQ at 800-492-6005 and, for Medicaid participants, the supports planner or case manager.
The RN Supervisor reviews participant direction and caregiver acceptance with the client at every supervisory visit and annual reassessment, and documents the review.

The Compliance Officer reviews all rejection, dismissal and reassignment records every quarter to check for retaliation, gaps in services and patterns by caregiver. Results go to the QA committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures participant direction is honored, prevents retaliation, investigates reports of it, and verifies that the plan of service names the agency.
Explains choice and participant direction at intake, confirms the participant's agency choice and gives written information.
Offers caregivers for acceptance, follows participants' scheduling preferences within authorized hours, and arranges replacements without service interruption.
Resolves conflicting instructions, reviews participant direction at visits, informs the supports planner or case manager of any gap, and documents rejections and dismissals.
Follows instructions from the participant and the other authorized sources, reports conflicts to the RN Supervisor, and does not retaliate.
Reviews rejection, dismissal and reassignment records every quarter.

Plan of service naming the agency
Caregiver acceptance or rejection and dismissal request records
Replacement assignment records with dates and times
Instruction conflict reports and resolutions

policies.title: Scope of Services — What Caregivers May and May Not Do
policies.applies_to: All clients, all caregivers (CNAs, CMTs, non-certified aides), the supervising RN, intake and scheduling staff
policies.purpose: To state exactly which services [AGENCY NAME] provides, which it does not, and who may perform each type of task, so that clients know what to expect, caregivers stay within their authority, and the services offered match the OHCQ license application and the Medicaid plan of service.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is a Residential Service Agency that employs or contracts workers to provide home health care services to unrelated sick or disabled persons in their homes. The agency provides only the services listed in its written Scope of Services Schedule, which must match the services checked on the agency's OHCQ application. For Medicaid participants under Community First Choice (CFC) and CPAS, personal assistance is limited to assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs) set out in the participant's plan of service and within the service budget based on assessed need. Escort and travel expenses are not covered, and housekeeping unrelated to ADLs is not covered; caregivers do not perform them under Medicaid hours. Nursing tasks are performed only by staff licensed or certified to perform them. Under CFC, delegated nursing tasks require a CNA and medication administration requires a CMT. The agency accepts clients with skilled needs (such as wound care, catheter care, ventilator care or infusion) only as stated in the Scope of Services Schedule and only after an RN assessment. Caregivers never perform a task outside the plan of care or plan of service, or outside their credential or delegation.

definitions.definition: An agency licensed by OHCQ that employs or contracts workers to provide at least one home health care service to an unrelated sick or disabled person in the person's home.
Activities of daily living, such as bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, mobility, grooming and eating, as defined in COMAR 10.07.05.02.
Instrumental activities of daily living that support independent living in the home, such as meal preparation and light housekeeping tied to the client's care, as defined in the regulations.
A service that requires the judgment and skill of a licensed nurse or other licensed professional, such as wound care, catheter care, ventilator care or infusion therapy.
A nursing task that the RN delegates, under COMAR 10.27.11, to a qualified CNA or CMT for a specific client.

definitions.term: Plan of service / plan of care
definitions.definition: The written document that lists the services authorized or ordered for the client, how often, and by whom.

procedures: The Administrator, with the Supervising RN, prepares a written Scope of Services Schedule listing every service the agency offers (for example ADL assistance, IADL assistance, medication assistance, delegated nursing tasks and any skilled services). The Administrator compares the schedule to the services checked on the OHCQ application before the application is submitted.

The Administrator decides in writing whether the agency accepts clients with skilled needs: [ACCEPTS / DOES NOT ACCEPT SKILLED NEEDS — ADMINISTRATOR TO SELECT]. If the agency accepts them, the schedule lists each skilled service accepted, the licensed staff who will provide it, and the requirement for an RN assessment within 48 hours (or 7 calendar days when the RN documents the reason, as provided in SVC-03).

The Administrator revises the schedule only after consulting the Supervising RN. Before the agency adds a service, the Administrator confirms the OHCQ license covers it, updates the application or notifies OHCQ as required, and records the change under GOV-03.
Intake staff give every prospective client a plain-language summary of the Scope of Services at first contact (SVC-02), and the Service Agreement (CR-06) refers to it.

For Medicaid participants, the Supervising RN and Scheduler confirm that every task scheduled matches a service in the plan of service and falls within the authorized hours and service budget. The agency does not provide Medicaid-billed services that are not in the plan.

The Supervising RN writes task instructions for each client from the plan of care or plan of service, listing the tasks the caregiver is to perform and the tasks the caregiver is not to perform. Task time planning uses the OLTSS Standardized Times for Assistance with ADLs, IADLs and Delegated Nursing Tasks.

The agency does not bill Medicaid for escort or travel time, or for housekeeping unrelated to ADLs. If a participant asks for these, the caregiver explains that they are not covered and tells the Supervising RN, who tells the supports planner or case manager if the participant wants to ask for a change in the plan (SVC-13).

Caregivers perform nursing tasks only when the Supervising RN has delegated the specific task for that client in writing and the caregiver holds the required credential. Under CFC, delegated nursing tasks require a CNA, and medication administration requires a CMT (SVC-04, SVC-05, SVC-06).

Caregivers do not perform tasks outside their training or credential. If a client asks for such a task, the caregiver declines politely, ensures the client is safe, and calls the Supervising RN or the on-call number (SVC-11) on the same day.

If a client's needs exceed the agency's Scope of Services, the Supervising RN tells the client or representative the same day, explains the options, and starts the process in SVC-12 if services cannot safely continue.

At orientation (PER-03), each caregiver receives the Scope of Services Schedule and a one-page 'May Do / May Not Do' list. The caregiver signs that it was received and understood, and the signature is filed in the personnel record.

Each year, as part of the QA review (GOV-04), the Administrator and Supervising RN review complaints, incident reports and supervisory visit findings for any caregiver work outside the scope. They correct the scope, training or assignments as needed.

A caregiver who knowingly performs services outside the scope, credential or delegation is subject to corrective action under PER-07. If the conduct may be grounds for Board of Nursing action, it is reported under PER-10.

responsibilities.duty: Approves and maintains the Scope of Services Schedule, ensures it matches the OHCQ application and license, and decides whether skilled needs are accepted.
Determines which tasks are appropriate for each client, delegates nursing tasks, writes task instructions, and responds to scope questions from staff.
Explains the scope of services to prospective clients and screens requests against the schedule.
Schedules only tasks and hours in the plan of care or plan of service.
Performs only the assigned tasks within credential and delegation, declines other tasks, and reports requests for out-of-scope services.

Comparison of the schedule to the OHCQ application, with date and initials
Written task instructions for each client

policies.title: Client Intake, Eligibility and Assessment
policies.applies_to: Intake staff, Supervising RN, Administrator, schedulers; all prospective private-pay and Medicaid (CFC/CPAS) clients
