We accept the lesser of our usual and customary charge to the general public or the Medicaid fee schedule rate. We keep service documentation for 6 years from the date of service. We do not remain a participant with an unpaid overpayment, and we refund overpayments promptly.

definitions.definition: The Department-approved telephonic timekeeping system used to document personal assistance visits and generate claims.
The rate [AGENCY NAME] charges the general public for the same service.

The Medicaid rate published by the Department. As of the FY 2025 transmittal (effective July 1, 2024), W5519 (CFC) and W5527 (CPAS) are $6.3962 per 15-minute unit. Shared attendant (W5521/W5528) is $4.2597 per 15 minutes. The daily rate for more than 12 hours per day (W5532) is $329.84.
Any Medicaid payment received that the agency was not entitled to, such as billing without documentation, for unauthorized services, or at the wrong rate or units.

procedures: Billing staff verify each month that the plan of service authorizes the hours and service codes to be billed and that the participant is Medicaid-eligible (see SVC-09).

Caregivers clock in and out through ISAS at the participant's home for every visit, as required in SVC-08. Time not captured in ISAS is not billed unless corrected under the Department's missing-time process and approved by the Administrator.
Billing staff review ISAS-generated claims weekly against the schedule, plan of service, authorized hours and visit documentation. They flag discrepancies before submission.
Billing staff bill for up to 12 hours per day in 15-minute units. For days over 12 hours, the daily rate applies. Staff do not combine or split units to increase payment.
Billing staff apply the shared attendant rate only when the plan of service authorizes shared attendant services and the visit meets those conditions.
Billing staff compare the rate billed with our usual and customary charge to the general public. Payment is the lesser of the two. The Administrator keeps the usual and customary rate sheet current.

Rates are expected to rise 3% each July 1 subject to the State budget, but the FY 2026 and FY 2027 rates were reported level. Each June, billing staff check the Department's current fee schedule and transmittals. The Administrator approves any rate update before it is entered.
Billing staff submit claims promptly, and never later than 12 months from the date of service. They track unpaid or rejected claims weekly and correct and resubmit within the time limit.

Billing staff never bill for services not in the plan of service, for visits that did not occur, for time a caregiver was not providing the authorized service, or in a way not covered by the provider agreement.
Billing staff retain visit and service documentation (dates and hours) for 6 years from the date of service and keep it retrievable for audits.
If any employee believes a claim was wrong, they report it at once to the Administrator. The Administrator opens an overpayment review within 5 business days and documents findings.

If an overpayment is confirmed, the Administrator stops further billing of the same issue. The Administrator refunds or voids and adjusts the claim through the Department's process promptly and records the date and amount.
The Administrator reviews how the error occurred and takes corrective action (training, system change, discipline). The Administrator reports the review to QA (see GOV-04).
Billing staff check monthly that no overpayment remains outstanding. The agency must not have unpaid overpayments to remain a provider.
The agency cooperates fully with Department reviews, audits and inspections, and gives records access as required (see GOV-08 and REC-03).
The Administrator does a monthly internal audit of a sample of claims against ISAS records, schedules, plan of service and caregiver notes, and logs results.

responsibilities.duty: Owns billing integrity, approves rate updates, directs overpayment reviews and refunds, and certifies audit results.
Review and submit claims accurately and on time, apply correct rates and units, and retain records for 6 years.
Schedule only authorized hours and correct missed or changed visits in the system.
Clock in and out in ISAS for each visit and provide only the authorized services.
Alerts billing staff to changes in plan of service or services delivered that affect billing.

documentation: ISAS visit and claim records
Weekly claim review and monthly audit logs
Current fee schedule and usual and customary rate sheet
Overpayment review files, refund or adjustment records, and corrective actions
Service documentation retained 6 years from date of service

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contract caregivers, supervisors, the Administrator and the Supervising RN
policies.purpose: To protect clients from abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation, to train staff to recognize and prevent them, and to make sure suspected cases are reported at once to the right authorities.
policies.policy: Clients of [AGENCY NAME] have the right to be free from mental, verbal, sexual and physical abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation. Training on prevention of abuse and neglect is required for every caregiver. Any employee who has reason to believe a client has been subjected to abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation must report immediately to the local department of social services (Adult Protective Services, or Child Protective Services for minors) under COMAR 07.02.16, and to the Administrator. We report the incident to the Department within 24 hours of knowledge and file the written report within 7 calendar days. Conduct that may be grounds for Board of Nursing action is reported immediately to the Board of Nursing and OHCQ. No one is retaliated against for reporting in good faith.

definitions.definition: Mental, verbal, sexual or physical harm or mistreatment of a client.
Failure to provide care, services or supervision needed to avoid physical harm or distress. Self-neglect is when the client does not meet their own basic needs.
Improper use of a client's money, property or resources for someone else's benefit.
Separating a client from others against their will or confining them to a room or area.
The local agency that receives reports of suspected abuse, neglect, self-neglect and exploitation (Adult Protective Services for adults, Child Protective Services for minors).

procedures: During orientation and annually, the Supervising RN or designee trains every caregiver on prevention of abuse and neglect, recognizing signs, and reporting duties. Training is recorded in the personnel file (see PER-03).
Before referral, the agency completes the screening required by COMAR 10.07.05.10, including criminal history checks, licensure or certification verification and references (see PER-02).

At admission, staff give each client or representative the written rights statement, which includes freedom from abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation. Staff also give the OHCQ complaint hotline (800-492-6005) and explain how to reach Adult or Child Protective Services. The client acknowledges receipt in writing (see CR-01).
Any employee who sees, suspects or is told of possible abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation first ensures the client's immediate safety. If the client is in danger, the employee calls 911.
The employee reports immediately by phone to the local department of social services at [LOCAL DSS PHONE]. The employee does not wait for proof, an investigation, or supervisor permission.

The employee then notifies the Supervising RN or the on-call RN at [PHONE] right away, and the Administrator the same day. If the suspected person is the Administrator or RN, the employee notifies the governing authority.

The Administrator removes any accused employee from the client's care immediately pending review. The Administrator notifies the client or representative, unless doing so would put the client at risk.

The Administrator reports the incident to the Department within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge. Staff complete the written report on the Department's designated form within 7 calendar days and keep a copy (see SAF-02).
If the conduct may be grounds for Board of Nursing action, the Administrator notifies the Board of Nursing and OHCQ immediately (see PER-10).

The agency investigates using the complaint investigation protocol: time, date, place, people involved, full description, disposition and follow-up to prevent recurrence. If no investigation is conducted, the reason is documented (see CR-02).
The Administrator cooperates with the local department of social services, law enforcement and OHCQ, and gives them records as required.
The Supervising RN reviews the care plan and visits for the affected client within 48 hours. The RN adds protective measures and arranges needed medical follow-up.
The Administrator informs the supports planner of Medicaid participants of the report and any service changes, following SVC-13.
Employees who report in good faith are not retaliated against. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination.
The Administrator reviews each report and its outcome, identifies trends and training needs, and includes them in QA review (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Report suspected abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation immediately to the local department of social services and to the agency.
Ensures timely external reports, removes accused staff from client care, oversees the investigation and notifies the Board of Nursing and OHCQ when required.
Assesses client safety, adjusts the plan of care, delivers abuse prevention training and notifies the Board when RN conduct is involved.
Receives and acts on reports that involve the Administrator.

documentation: Training records on abuse and neglect prevention
Client rights acknowledgments and OHCQ hotline notice
Report to the local department of social services (date, time, person contacted)
24-hour notification and 7-day written report
Investigation report and follow-up
Notices to the Board of Nursing and OHCQ

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contract caregivers, supervisors, the Supervising RN and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To ensure incidents and complaints are identified, recorded, reported to the Department within required time frames, followed up and used to improve safety.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports incidents and complaints to the Department within 24 hours of knowledge of the event, and submits a written report within 7 calendar days on the form designated by the Department. Suspected abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation is also reported immediately to the local department of social services. Medication errors and adverse drug reactions are recorded in the client record with corrective action. Known conduct that may be grounds for Board of Nursing action is reported immediately to the Board of Nursing and OHCQ. All incidents are aggregated for quality assurance review.

definitions.definition: Any unusual event involving a client or caregiver that affects or could affect health or safety, such as a fall, injury, medication error, adverse reaction, missing client, property loss or damage, allegation of misconduct, or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation.
The time any agency employee first learns of the incident or complaint.
The written incident report form the Department specifies for the 7-day report.

procedures: A caregiver who witnesses or learns of an incident first ensures the client's safety. The caregiver calls 911 for emergencies and follows SVC-10.
The caregiver reports the incident by phone to the Supervising RN or the on-call RN at [PHONE] immediately and no later than the end of the shift.
The RN who receives the report records the time of knowledge in the incident log. The 24-hour reporting clock runs from this time or from earlier knowledge by any employee.
If suspected abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation is involved, staff follow SAF-01 and call the local department of social services immediately at [LOCAL DSS PHONE].
The Administrator notifies the Department of the incident or complaint within 24 hours of knowledge and records the date, time, method and the name of the person contacted.
The caregiver and RN complete an internal incident report the same day. It states date, time, place, people involved, what happened, actions taken and client status.
The Administrator completes and submits the written report on the Department's designated form within 7 calendar days and keeps a copy in the incident file.

The Supervising RN notifies the client or representative, and the physician if needed, and documents the notification. For Medicaid participants, the RN also informs the supports planner (see SVC-13).

For a medication error or adverse drug reaction, the RN assesses the client, contacts the prescriber or physician when needed, and records the error or reaction and corrective action in the client record (see SVC-06).
If the incident involves conduct that may be grounds for Board of Nursing action, the Administrator notifies the Board of Nursing and OHCQ immediately (see PER-10).
The Administrator investigates each incident, determines the cause, and documents disposition and follow-up to prevent recurrence. If no investigation is done, the reason is documented.
For complaints, staff follow CR-02 and use the same 24-hour and 7-day reporting timelines to the Department.
The Administrator gives investigation reports to OHCQ immediately on request.
The Administrator updates the care plan, schedule, training or discipline based on findings and confirms completion within 14 days.
Each month, the Administrator compiles the incident log by type, client, caregiver, time and cause, and presents trends at the QA meeting (see GOV-04).
The Administrator keeps incident records for the retention period in REC-01 and has them available for inspection.

responsibilities.duty: Secure safety, report every incident immediately to the RN or on-call, and complete the internal report.
Receives reports, logs time of knowledge, assesses the client, notifies the client, physician and supports planner, and documents medication errors and corrective action.
Submits the 24-hour notice and 7-day written report, notifies the local department of social services, Board of Nursing and OHCQ as required, and directs investigation and corrective action.
Reviews aggregated incident data and tracks corrective actions.

documentation: Incident log with time of knowledge
Internal incident reports
24-hour notification record and 7-day Department form
Investigation findings and follow-up
Medication error and adverse reaction entries in the client record
Notices to local department of social services, Board of Nursing and OHCQ
Monthly aggregate incident report

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, the Supervising RN, trainers, schedulers and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To reduce the risk of infection for clients and employees, and to set required procedures for infection control, disposal of biomedical waste, and protection of employees from occupational exposure.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains written infection control procedures and procedures for disposal of biomedical waste, as COMAR 10.07.05.08 requires. Training includes standard precautions for infection control. We give employees personal protective equipment (PPE) and handwashing supplies and keep a bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan consistent with the OSHA standard where aides have occupational exposure. TB screening is part of caregiver screening before referral. No separate COMAR 10.07.05 section on vaccinations was verified, so any vaccine requirement is based on OSHA rules, client or payor requirements, or agency policy.

definitions.definition: Basic infection prevention practices applied to every client, including hand hygiene, gloves and PPE, safe handling of sharps, and respiratory hygiene.
Waste generated in care that may be contaminated with blood or body fluids, such as sharps and soiled dressings.
Personal protective equipment such as gloves, masks, gowns and eye protection.
Reasonably anticipated contact with blood or other potentially infectious material during an employee's duties.

procedures: The Supervising RN designs and reviews these infection control procedures annually and after any exposure event or outbreak. The Administrator approves changes (see GOV-03).

During orientation, before first client contact, the RN or trainer instructs and observes caregivers on standard precautions: hand hygiene, glove use, PPE, cleaning and disinfecting, safe handling of laundry, and respiratory etiquette. Training is recorded in the personnel file (see PER-03).
The Administrator ensures caregivers receive an initial supply of PPE and handwashing supplies and re-supplies on request. Staff do not charge employees for PPE.
Caregivers perform hand hygiene before and after each client contact, after removing gloves, and after contact with body fluids.
Caregivers wear gloves for contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin or soiled items, and add other PPE as the task requires. They remove PPE safely and do not reuse single-use items.

Caregivers do not provide care while symptomatic with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, undiagnosed rash or other contagious symptoms. They call the Supervising RN or scheduler so coverage can be arranged (see PER-04).
The agency assesses TB screening in caregiver pre-referral screening, as set out in PER-04 and PER-02. Results are kept in the personnel or screening file.
Caregivers do not handle sharps beyond the scope of their tasks. Where sharps are present, they use a puncture-resistant container, never recap or bend needles, and do not reach into containers.
Caregivers dispose of biomedical waste per instructions from the Supervising RN and in accordance with applicable State and local requirements. Staff report any questions about disposal to the RN.

The Administrator maintains a written bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan where aides have occupational exposure. It covers exposure determination, PPE, training, labeling, and post-exposure evaluation and follow-up, and the plan is reviewed annually in line with 29 CFR 1910.1030.

After any needlestick or exposure to blood or body fluids, the caregiver washes the area, ends the task safely, and calls the Supervising RN or on-call RN at [PHONE] immediately. The RN arranges prompt medical evaluation.
The Administrator documents each exposure, evaluation and follow-up confidentially, and reports as required under SAF-02.
If a client has a known or suspected communicable illness, the RN adds precautions to the plan of care and instructs caregivers before the next visit. Client privacy is maintained under CR-03.
Caregivers clean and disinfect reusable client equipment between uses as instructed in training and plan of care. They report any equipment they cannot clean safely.
The Supervising RN conducts infection control checks during supervisory visits and documents findings (see SVC-04).
The QA Committee reviews exposure incidents, reported infections and staff illness trends at least quarterly (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts procedures, supplies PPE, maintains the exposure control plan and ensures training.
Develops and updates procedures, trains and observes caregivers, manages post-exposure follow-up and adds precautions to care plans.
Follow standard precautions, use PPE, stay home when sick, and report exposures and equipment problems.
Reviews infection-related events and corrective actions.

documentation: Written infection control and biomedical waste procedures
Training records on standard precautions
PPE and supply records
TB screening results in personnel or screening file
Exposure control plan and exposure incident records
Supervisory visit infection control observations

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Supervising RN, on-call staff, schedulers and caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] has emergency procedures, knows which clients are at greatest risk in an emergency or disaster, and can keep in contact with clients and staff and continue essential services.
policies.policy: Emergency procedures are a required policy under COMAR 10.07.05.08, and [AGENCY NAME] maintains them in this policy. No separate RSA emergency-preparedness section was found. We rank clients by risk, record an emergency contact for each, and maintain a call tree. The 24/7 on-call line stays in operation in emergencies, with response within 1 hour as COMAR 10.07.05.12 requires. The assessment timing exceptions for weather-related emergencies, natural disasters and federal, state or local emergency declarations apply to assessments only. They do not excuse caregivers' service duties.

definitions.definition: Any event, such as severe weather, power outage, fire, flood, public health emergency or declared disaster, that threatens client safety or disrupts services.

A tiered list of clients by how much they depend on agency services and how vulnerable they would be to disruption (for example, oxygen or electrically powered equipment, no family support, cognitive impairment or inability to evacuate).
A written sequence of who calls whom in an emergency, with phone numbers, so all clients and staff can be reached.
The agency's 24/7 contact number with an RN or designee who responds within 1 hour.

procedures: At the initial assessment and at least annually, the Supervising RN records for each client: emergency contact, representative, physician, medical equipment or oxygen needs, mobility and cognitive limits, and whether the client can evacuate. The RN enters this in the client record (see SVC-03).
The Supervising RN assigns each client a risk tier (high, medium, low) and records it in the emergency client list. The list is updated when a client's condition or status changes.

The Administrator maintains the call tree with current numbers for clients, representatives, caregivers, supervisors, on-call RN, the supports planner for Medicaid participants, and emergency services. The Administrator reviews it every quarter.

At admission, the RN reviews emergency steps with the client or representative. The RN gives the 24/7 on-call number [PHONE] in writing and shares information on emergency contacts and, when appropriate, personal emergency response systems (see CR-01 and SVC-11).

Before foreseeable emergencies such as storms, the Administrator or RN activates the plan, contacts high-risk clients first, confirms their emergency contact and needs, and confirms caregiver availability and coverage.
Schedulers reassign visits to prioritize high-risk clients whose caregivers cannot reach them, and notify clients of changes. Missed-visit procedures in SVC-07 apply.

During an emergency, caregivers in a client's home follow the client's emergency instructions, call 911 for life-threatening situations, and then notify the on-call RN. Caregivers do not put themselves in danger (see SAF-05).
The on-call line remains staffed throughout the emergency. The agency logs each call with date, time, caller, concern, response time and action taken. The response target is 1 hour (see SVC-11).

If an emergency prevents a required assessment from happening on time, the RN documents the reason and the emergency, and completes the assessment as soon as it is safe. The exception applies to assessments only, and caregivers continue all required service duties.

The RN contacts the client's supports planner or other resources for Medicaid participants who cannot be served, or who need alternative arrangements. Staff may refer clients to Maryland Access Point at 1-844-MAP-LINK for community resources.
The Administrator reports emergency-related incidents to the Department as required in SAF-02 and notifies OHCQ if the agency cannot operate.
After each activation, the Administrator and RN hold a review, document what worked and what did not, and correct the plan. The review is brought to the QA Committee (see GOV-04).
The Administrator tests the call tree at least annually and trains staff on this policy at orientation and annually (see PER-03).
The Administrator reviews and updates this policy at least annually (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the call tree, activates the plan, keeps the on-call line operating and makes reports to the Department and OHCQ.
Identifies and ranks client risk, reviews emergency steps with clients, prioritizes high-risk clients and documents assessment delays.
Reassign visits, notify clients and log changes during emergencies.
Answer the 24/7 line, respond within 1 hour and log every call.
Follow emergency procedures, protect safety, call 911 when needed and report to the on-call RN.

documentation: Client emergency contact and risk tier list
Current call tree and test records
Emergency plan activation records
On-call call log
Documentation of delayed assessments and the reason
Post-emergency review and corrective actions

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, nurses, supervisors, office staff, and contract caregivers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect caregivers and clients from injury, violence, harassment and occupational exposure while services are delivered in client homes and agency offices. To meet the agency's duty to maintain environment and safety policies and to carry workers' compensation coverage.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written environment and safety policy and applies it to every client home and to agency workplaces. The RN assesses home safety at intake, and the plan of care or plan of service includes safety measures to protect against injury. Every caregiver has the right to stop work and leave a home that is unsafe, and will not be disciplined or retaliated against for doing so in good faith. The agency does not tolerate violence, threats or harassment by clients, family members, visitors, co-workers or supervisors. The agency carries workers' compensation insurance for all employees and reports workplace injuries as required. The agency follows federal bloodborne pathogens standards and the OSH Act General Duty Clause to provide a workplace free of recognized hazards likely to cause serious harm.

definitions.definition: Any condition in or around the home that presents a reasonable risk of injury or illness to the caregiver or client. Examples include threats or violence, weapons displayed in a threatening way, fire or structural hazards, gas or carbon monoxide odor, infestations, hazardous clutter, unrestrained aggressive animals, and impairment-related behavior that endangers others.
Any act or threat of physical violence, intimidation, stalking, or verbal or non-verbal abuse directed at a caregiver or staff member while working.
Unwelcome conduct, including sexual, racial or other discriminatory conduct, that creates an intimidating, hostile or offensive working condition.
Reasonably anticipated contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials during the performance of duties.

procedures: At intake, the RN completes a home safety assessment as part of the in-home assessment. It covers entrances and lighting, fire and smoke detection, trip and fall hazards, utilities, pets, weapons, infestations, smoking or oxygen use, and known behavioral risks. The RN records the result in the clinical record.
The RN writes safety measures into the plan of care or plan of service to protect the client and caregiver from injury. The RN gives the caregiver those measures before the first visit.
Before the first visit, the scheduler tells the caregiver of any known risk, including behavior history and a client's refusal to secure animals.

Where a hazard can be corrected, the RN or Administrator discusses it with the client or representative, documents the discussion, and sets a date for correction. Services continue during correction only if the RN judges it safe.
Every caregiver receives training at orientation and annually on home safety, body mechanics, de-escalation, recognizing warning signs of violence, bloodborne pathogens and how to report hazards.

A caregiver who believes the home is unsafe may leave at any time. Before leaving, the caregiver makes sure the client is not left in immediate danger. If the client is in danger, the caregiver calls 911 or the appropriate emergency service.

The caregiver calls the 24/7 on-call line at [PHONE] as soon as it is safe and reports the situation. The on-call nurse or supervisor decides next steps, including how to secure client care and whether the visit is rescheduled, reassigned or suspended.

In any threat of immediate harm to the caregiver, the caregiver calls 911 first and the agency second. The agency does not require a caregiver to remain in a home to finish a shift or to avoid a missed visit.

Caregivers report every incident of violence, threats, harassment, injury or exposure to the supervisor or on-call nurse by the end of the shift. They may report to the Administrator directly if the supervisor is involved. The agency completes an incident report under SAF-02 within the same business day.

For any injury or illness arising from work, the caregiver reports it by the end of the shift. The supervisor makes sure the employee gets medical care and the Administrator notifies the workers' compensation carrier and files any report the Workers' Compensation Commission requires within the time it sets.

After a bloodborne pathogen exposure, the caregiver washes the area right away, reports it to the supervisor, and is referred for confidential medical evaluation and follow-up under 29 CFR 1910.1030. The agency documents the exposure incident and the evaluation, and the caregiver's medical records remain confidential.

The Administrator or RN reviews each reported violence, harassment or unsafe-home event within 2 business days. The review decides whether to adjust the plan of care, change staffing (such as two-person visits), set conditions for services, or begin discharge or suspension under SVC-12.
If a client or family member's conduct involves possible abuse, neglect or exploitation, or a crime, the Administrator also follows SAF-01 and contacts law enforcement as appropriate.

Complaints of harassment or violence by a co-worker or supervisor go to the Administrator and are investigated promptly. The agency takes corrective action and tells the reporter the matter has been addressed, within confidentiality limits.

The agency does not retaliate against anyone who reports a hazard, leaves an unsafe home in good faith, files a workers' compensation claim, or reports violence or harassment. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination.

The Administrator reviews all safety incidents, injuries and exposures at least quarterly, identifies trends, and takes the findings to the quality assurance process under GOV-04. The Administrator also confirms that workers' compensation coverage is active and renews it before expiration.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the safety program, workers' compensation coverage, injury reporting and the no-retaliation commitment. Reviews safety trends at least quarterly.
Completes the home safety assessment, writes safety measures into the plan of care, and decides on service changes after a safety event.
Shares known risks before visits and responds to caregiver safety calls 24/7.
Follows safety measures, uses protective equipment, leaves unsafe homes, and reports hazards, injuries, exposures and threats by the end of the shift.

documentation: Home safety assessment in the clinical record
Safety measures in the plan of care or plan of service
Incident reports for violence, harassment, injury and exposure
Workers' compensation policy and injury reports
Exposure incident and post-exposure evaluation records (confidential)
Training records on safety and bloodborne pathogens
Quarterly safety trend review summaries

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, nurses, schedulers and contract caregivers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To state clearly whether caregivers may drive clients, to protect clients and caregivers from transport risk, and to prevent billing for services that Medicaid does not cover.
policies.policy: Client transportation is not a service [AGENCY NAME] provides in the ordinary course of care. Caregivers do not drive clients in their own vehicles, agency vehicles or any other vehicle unless the Administrator has approved it in writing in advance for that client. Where approval is given, the caregiver must hold a valid driver's license, the vehicle must be insured, and the client or representative must sign a transport consent form. Medicaid personal assistance covers ADL and IADL help according to the plan of service, but escort and travel expenses are not covered. The agency never bills Medicaid for time spent transporting a client or for travel expenses. In an emergency, caregivers call 911 and do not transport the client.

definitions.definition: Driving a client, or having a client ride in a vehicle driven by the caregiver, for any purpose.
Accompanying a client to an appointment or outing. Escort and travel expenses are not covered Medicaid personal assistance, so the agency does not bill them to Medicaid.
Liability insurance protecting the agency when an employee uses a personally owned vehicle for agency business.
A written agreement signed by the client or representative that acknowledges the risks and conditions of transport and permits the specific trip.

procedures: At orientation and on the service agreement, the agency tells every client and caregiver that caregivers do not transport clients unless approved in writing under this policy.
A caregiver who is asked to drive a client declines politely, explains the policy, and tells the supervisor. The caregiver does not drive the client even if the client or family insists.

A client or representative who wants transport help may ask the RN or Administrator. The RN reviews whether it is consistent with the plan of service and the client's needs. The agency also encourages use of Medicaid non-emergency transportation, paratransit, family or other community options.

The Administrator may approve transport only for a specific client and purpose, in writing, when it is consistent with the plan of service, the caregiver is willing, and the requirements below are met. The approval states the dates, destination and who may drive.

Before approval, the Administrator verifies and copies the caregiver's current driver's license, confirms the vehicle's registration and liability insurance, and checks that the caregiver has no disqualifying driving history under agency standards.
The agency carries non-owned auto liability coverage. COMAR sets no minimum liability amount, so the Administrator reviews the coverage amount with the agency's insurance broker at least annually.
Before the first trip, the client or representative signs the transport consent form. The agency keeps it in the clinical record and renews it at least annually.

During approved transport, the caregiver obeys all traffic laws, wears a seat belt, does not use a hand-held phone, makes sure the client is secured with a seat belt and has the proper assistive equipment, and never transports a client who is acutely ill or unsafe to move.

Time spent transporting a client, escorting or traveling is not billed to Medicaid. Visit time billed to Medicaid is limited to time spent delivering personal assistance under the plan of service. EVV clock-in and clock-out follow SVC-08.
For private-pay clients, any charge for approved transport must be set out in the service agreement under CR-06 before the trip.
Mileage reimbursement for caregiver use of a personal vehicle is handled under PER-06 and is never charged to Medicaid or paid by the client.
In a medical emergency, the caregiver calls 911, stays with the client, and follows SVC-10. The caregiver does not drive the client to the hospital.

If a crash, injury or property damage occurs during transport, the caregiver calls 911 if needed and notifies the on-call supervisor. The agency completes an incident report under SAF-02 and notifies the insurer.

The agency removes transport approval from any caregiver whose license is suspended, whose insurance lapses, or who has an at-fault crash or traffic violation affecting safety. The Administrator documents the action.
The Administrator reviews transport approvals, consent forms and incidents at least annually and reports to the quality assurance committee under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Approves or denies any transport in writing, verifies license and insurance, maintains non-owned auto coverage, and reviews transport activity annually.
Reviews transport requests against the plan of service and the client's condition and advises on alternatives.
Does not transport clients without written approval, and follows safe driving and consent requirements if approved.
Makes sure transport, escort and travel time is never billed to Medicaid.

documentation: Written Administrator transport approval
Transport consent form signed by the client or representative
Copy of the caregiver's driver's license, vehicle registration and insurance
Non-owned auto liability policy
Incident reports for transport-related events
Annual review of transport activity

policies.title: Caregiver Qualifications, Certification (CNA/CMT) and License Verification
policies.applies_to: All employees, independent contractors and contract caregivers who provide services for [AGENCY NAME], and the staff who hire, assign and supervise them
policies.purpose: To make sure that only qualified individuals, with verified licensure or certification, are referred to clients, and that certified caregivers are assigned when a client's needs require one.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] verifies each individual's professional license or certification before referral and obtains written verification of the qualifications of everyone who renders services. A certified caregiver (CNA, and for medications a CMT) is assigned whenever the client needs one for ADLs or for medication administration. Under Community First Choice, a worker who administers medications must be a CMT, and a worker who performs other delegated nursing functions must also be a CNA. A non-certified caregiver is assigned only in the cases the regulation allows, and never to administer medications or perform delegated nursing tasks. The agency employs an RN who assesses new participants, delegates nursing tasks and instructs workers. A participant's representative is never assigned as the participant's worker. Conduct that may be grounds for Board of Nursing action is reported immediately to the Board and OHCQ.

definitions.definition: Certified nursing assistant, certified by the Maryland Board of Nursing.
Certified medication technician, certified by the Maryland Board of Nursing to administer medications under delegation.

A personal care aide who does not hold a CNA or CMT certificate. A non-certified caregiver may be provided only if the client needs no ADL help, needs ADL help only where the supervising nurse judges there are no predictable adverse health consequences, or has signed a waiver of skilled services.
Written confirmation, kept by the agency, of a worker's license or certification, training and other required qualifications.
Assignment by the RN of a nursing task to a qualified CNA or CMT under Board of Nursing delegation rules.

procedures: Human Resources identifies the role and qualifications required for each position in the job description (PER-09) before recruiting.

Before any referral, Human Resources verifies in writing the status of each CNA or CMT certification, and of any nursing license, with the Maryland Board of Nursing's online verification. The verification is printed or saved with the date, the verifier's name and the status.

Human Resources checks that the status is current and in good standing with no restriction or discipline. Anyone with an inactive, expired, suspended or restricted credential is not referred in that capacity.

For every individual who will render services, Human Resources obtains and files written verification of qualifications, covering training, certification or licensure, and the pre-referral screening under PER-02.
Human Resources completes the pre-referral screening and skills assessment under PER-02 and PER-03 before the worker is added to the list available for assignment.

The RN assigns staff after the in-home assessment. The RN decides whether the client needs a certified caregiver for ADLs, or medication administration, and documents the reasons in the clinical record.

Where a CMT is required for medication administration, the scheduler assigns only a CMT. Where the RN delegates another nursing function, the scheduler assigns only a CNA who holds the CMT where required, as the RN's delegation specifies.

A non-certified caregiver is assigned only if the RN documents that the client needs no ADL help, or needs ADL help with no predictable adverse health consequences in the RN's judgment, or the client has signed a waiver of skilled services under CR-07. The waiver is checked before the first visit.
The scheduler confirms the worker's credential status in the assignment record before each new assignment and does not assign a worker whose credential has lapsed.

Human Resources tracks credential expiration dates. It re-verifies each credential before expiration and at least once a year, and removes the worker from assignment on the date any credential lapses until verified again.

The RN gives each worker instruction on the plan of service and delegated tasks. The worker also accepts instruction on the plan of service from the participant or representative, the nurse monitor, a treating physician or NP, or the Maryland Department of Health.
The scheduler never assigns a participant's representative as that participant's worker. At intake the RN identifies the representative and records it in the clinical record.
If a subcontracted agency supplies a caregiver, the agency obtains evidence that the subcontractor has verified the personnel information, as required under GOV-09, before the caregiver is assigned.

Any employee who knows of conduct by a nurse, CNA or CMT that may be grounds for Board of Nursing action tells the Administrator immediately. The Administrator reports it immediately to the Board of Nursing and OHCQ as set out in PER-10.

The Administrator audits a sample of personnel files and assignment records at least quarterly for verification dates, credential status and assignment match, and takes the results to the quality assurance process in GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure only qualified individuals are referred, and reports reportable conduct to the Board of Nursing and OHCQ.
Verifies and tracks licenses and certifications and keeps written qualification verification.
Decides the caregiver certification level needed, delegates nursing tasks, and instructs workers.
Assigns only workers with the credential the RN specifies and never assigns a participant's representative as worker.

documentation: Board of Nursing verification printouts with date and verifier
Written verification of qualifications in each personnel file
Credential expiration tracking log
RN documentation of caregiver level needed in the clinical record
Signed waiver of skilled services, where applicable
Subcontractor verification evidence
Reports to the Board of Nursing and OHCQ

policies.title: Criminal History Records Checks and Pre-Referral Screening
policies.applies_to: All applicants, employees, independent contractors and contract caregivers, including nurses, who will provide direct services for [AGENCY NAME], and the staff who screen them
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual completes required screening before being referred to a client, and to protect clients from harm and the agency from ineligible workers.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes a State criminal history records check (or a private agency background check) before referral of any individual, under Health-General Title 19, Subtitle 19. Under Community First Choice, checks are required for all direct service workers, including nurses. Before referral, pre-referral screening also includes licensure or certification verification, a basic health screening including TB, references, employment history, a Form I-9, identity and employment eligibility verification, an in-person interview, and a skills assessment and demonstration. As agency policy, the agency also screens against the OIG exclusion list and the Maryland Medicaid exclusion list. No individual is referred to a client until every element is complete and reviewed. Screening records are kept in the agency's business office.

definitions.definition: The set of checks that must be completed before an individual is referred to a client.
A State criminal history records check, or a private agency background check, of a direct service worker under Health-General Title 19, Subtitle 19.
Any individual who provides hands-on or in-home services to clients, including nurses, aides, and contract caregivers.
The U.S. HHS Office of Inspector General List of Excluded Individuals/Entities and the Maryland Medicaid list of excluded or suspended providers.

procedures: Human Resources gives each applicant the application and tells them that employment is conditional on completing all screening. The applicant is not scheduled with any client until screening is finished.

Human Resources starts the criminal history records check as soon as an offer is made. The applicant signs the required consent and provides fingerprints or the information needed for the State or private agency check, as the process requires.

Human Resources reviews the check result when it comes back. Any record found is referred to the Administrator, who makes the determination under Health-General Title 19, Subtitle 19 and, where needed, consults OHCQ. The decision and reasons are documented.
Human Resources checks identity and employment eligibility, and completes the Form I-9 within the federal deadlines. The agency keeps the I-9 as federal law requires.
Human Resources verifies licensure or certification (CNA, CMT, nursing license) under PER-01 and records the result.

Human Resources obtains and documents employment history, and contacts references. The reference check is recorded with the date, the person contacted and what was said. Unresolved discrepancies are referred to the Administrator.
The Administrator or RN conducts an in-person interview and records the results.
The applicant completes a basic health screening including TB under PER-04. Results are placed in the personnel file.

The RN conducts a skills assessment and demonstration of personal care and other skills, as described in PER-03, before the applicant is referred. Any applicant who does not demonstrate competency is not referred until retrained and reassessed.

Human Resources screens each applicant against the OIG exclusion list and the Maryland Medicaid exclusion list before hire. The agency repeats this screening for all staff at least monthly and records the date and result. Anyone found on an exclusion list is removed from client contact immediately and the Administrator follows GOV-05.

Human Resources completes a screening checklist for each person showing every element with its date and the reviewer's initials. The Administrator signs the checklist as complete before the individual is added to the referral pool.

Employees and contractors must tell Human Resources within 2 business days of any arrest, charge, conviction, or exclusion or licensure action. The Administrator then reviews continued eligibility and, if needed, repeats the criminal history check.
For subcontracted caregivers, the agency obtains written evidence that the subcontractor has verified the same personnel information before assignment, as required by GOV-09.
The agency keeps all screening records in its business office, in a secure, access-limited file. They are available to OHCQ, the Maryland Department of Health and auditors on request.
The Administrator audits a sample of screening files at least quarterly to check that every element was completed before the first referral date, and reports the results under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Makes eligibility determinations on any criminal history findings, approves completed screening, and manages exclusion findings.
Runs all screening elements, completes the checklist, performs monthly exclusion screening and secures the records.
Conducts the skills assessment and demonstration and, where assigned, the interview.
Provides complete and truthful information, completes required checks and reports changes within 2 business days.

documentation: Criminal history records check results and eligibility determination
Pre-referral screening checklist signed by the Administrator
I-9 and identity and employment eligibility documents
References and employment history records
Interview record
Health screening and TB results
Skills assessment and demonstration record
OIG and Maryland Medicaid exclusion screening logs
Subcontractor verification evidence

policies.title: Orientation, Competency Evaluation and Annual Training
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, nurses, contract caregivers and supervisory staff of [AGENCY NAME], and the staff who train and evaluate them
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual referred to clients is appropriately trained and has demonstrated skills before referral, and that skills are maintained through retraining.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides orientation and a skills assessment and demonstration before any individual is referred to a client. Training includes at minimum: instruction and supervised practice in personal care; recognizing situations that need RN referral, including a significant change in condition; record keeping; ethics and confidentiality; CPR; standard precautions; and prevention of abuse and neglect. Outside trainers must have OHCQ's written approval before they train for the agency. The agency keeps training records in each personnel file. COMAR 10.07.05.11 sets no annual number of training hours, so the annual refresher in this policy is agency policy. The RN trains and retrains staff whenever indicated.

definitions.definition: Initial training given before referral that covers the minimum content areas and the agency's policies.
Direct observation by the RN of the worker performing personal care tasks to confirm competency before referral to clients.
Hands-on practice of personal care tasks with direct observation and feedback from a qualified trainer or the RN.
A trainer or training program outside the agency that holds OHCQ's written approval to train.
Agency-required yearly review of the minimum content areas with a repeat skills check.

procedures: Human Resources schedules each new hire for orientation before the first client assignment. No individual is referred to a client until orientation and the skills assessment are complete.

Orientation covers the agency's policies, client rights, scope of services, the service agreement and plan of service, documentation, EVV, and the other topics Human Resources assigns, along with the minimum content in the next steps.

The RN or another qualified trainer teaches personal care and gives supervised practice in the following: bathing, toileting, transferring, positioning, dressing, grooming, feeding, mobility and other ADLs and IADLs the agency provides. Each trainee practices under supervision until competent.
The trainer teaches how to recognize situations that need RN referral, including a significant change in a client's condition, and how to report them right away under SVC-10.
The trainer teaches record keeping, including accurate service documentation, EVV clock-in and clock-out, and the monthly participant signature process.
The trainer teaches ethics and confidentiality, including privacy under CR-03 and professional boundaries under PER-07.
Every worker completes CPR training and holds a current CPR credential from a recognized provider. Human Resources records the expiration date and tracks renewal.
The trainer teaches standard precautions, including hand hygiene and personal protective equipment under SAF-03, and the prevention and reporting of abuse and neglect under SAF-01.

After instruction, the RN conducts and documents a skills assessment and demonstration of each core personal care skill. The record lists each skill, the date, the result and the RN's signature. A worker who does not demonstrate competency receives retraining and reassessment before referral.

If the agency uses an outside trainer or training program, the Administrator first obtains OHCQ's written approval and keeps a copy. No training from an unapproved outside trainer counts toward the agency's requirements.

Human Resources places training records in each employee's personnel file, including dates, topics, trainer, hours and results. Attendance sign-in sheets and competency checklists are kept with the file.

As agency policy, every caregiver completes an annual refresher on all the minimum content areas and repeats the skills demonstration, with the RN observing, within 12 months of the last assessment. Human Resources tracks due dates and does not assign a worker whose annual refresher is overdue past a 30-day grace period set by the Administrator.

The RN trains and retrains workers whenever indicated, including when a client's plan changes, a new task or device is introduced, a supervisory visit shows a gap, or an incident or complaint shows a training need. The retraining is documented in the personnel file.
The RN gives client-specific instruction before the first visit and whenever the plan of service changes, and records it.
The Administrator reviews training completion rates, skill assessment results and retraining needs quarterly and takes the findings to the quality assurance process under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the training program, obtains OHCQ approval for any outside trainer, and makes sure no one is referred before training and assessment are complete.
Provides or oversees training, conducts the skills assessment and demonstration, and trains and retrains staff when indicated.
Schedules orientation, tracks CPR and annual refresher due dates, and files training records in personnel files.
Completes all required training, demonstrates competency, and keeps CPR current.

documentation: Orientation agenda, sign-in sheets and attendance records
Skills assessment and demonstration checklist signed by the RN
CPR certificates and expiration tracking
OHCQ written approval for any outside trainer
Annual refresher records
Retraining records and client-specific instruction records
Training records in each personnel file

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees, independent contractors and contract caregivers of [AGENCY NAME] who will have contact with clients, and the staff who administer this policy
policies.purpose: To protect clients and staff from communicable disease by requiring health screening, including TB screening, before referral, and to meet the requirement for an employee health policy.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires a basic health screening, including TB screening, before an individual is referred to a client. Employee health requirements are part of the agency's required policies. COMAR 10.07.05.10 sets no re-screening frequency in the text the agency has relied on, so the re-screening schedule below is agency policy. The agency follows the federal bloodborne pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, for staff with occupational exposure. Health results are kept in the personnel file in the business office, handled as confidential medical information, and used only for the purposes of this policy.

definitions.definition: A health evaluation, including TB screening, completed before referral to confirm the individual can perform the job safely without posing a communicable disease risk to clients.
Tuberculosis screening by a licensed health care provider using a recognized method, such as a skin test, blood test or, where applicable, a symptom review with follow-up.
An illness that can be transmitted from one person to another, including infectious TB, influenza, COVID-19, and other conditions of concern.
Reasonably anticipated contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials while performing duties.

procedures: Human Resources tells every applicant in the job offer that a basic health screening including TB screening is required before the first referral to a client.

The applicant has the screening completed by a licensed health care provider or public health clinic and gives the result to Human Resources. The result states the screening method and date, the finding, and any restrictions or whether the individual is able to work with clients.

Human Resources reviews the result before referral. If the screening is not complete, shows active or suspected TB, or states a restriction, the individual is not referred to a client. The Administrator is notified and decides next steps.

An individual with a positive TB result must provide written clearance from a licensed health care provider or the local health department that the individual is not infectious before referral or before returning to work.
Human Resources files all results in the personnel file kept in the business office. Medical information is kept in a confidential section accessible only to authorized staff.

As agency policy, each worker completes an annual health review. It includes a TB symptom questionnaire, and TB testing is repeated if there are symptoms, a known exposure, or direction from the local health department or the Administrator. Human Resources tracks the dates and gives the worker written notice 30 days before each is due.
A worker who is overdue for the annual review is not scheduled with clients after a 30-day grace period until it is completed.

Workers must tell their supervisor at once about symptoms of a communicable disease, including persistent cough, fever, night sweats or unexplained weight loss, and about any exposure to a diagnosed communicable disease. The supervisor tells the Administrator, who decides whether the worker should stay away from clients.

The Administrator notifies the local health department of reportable communicable diseases as required by law and cooperates with the health department's investigation, protecting employee privacy as the law allows.

The Administrator determines which positions have occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials. For those positions the agency provides bloodborne pathogens training, personal protective equipment, hepatitis B vaccination offered at no cost to the employee, and post-exposure evaluation and follow-up, as 29 CFR 1910.1030 requires.
After an exposure incident, the employee reports it right away. The agency arranges confidential medical evaluation and follow-up and documents the incident under SAF-05 and SAF-02.

Staff must stay home when ill with symptoms of a communicable disease and report to the supervisor. The scheduler arranges replacement coverage under SVC-07 without penalty to the employee, consistent with leave rules in PER-06.
The agency makes reasonable accommodation under applicable law where a health condition affects a worker's ability to perform the job, and does not discriminate on the basis of a health condition.
The Administrator reviews screening completion and re-screening compliance at least quarterly and reports the results under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Decides on work restrictions, reports communicable diseases as required, and oversees the bloodborne pathogens program.
Collects and reviews results before referral, tracks re-screening dates, and keeps medical records confidential in the personnel file.
Receives reports of symptoms or exposure and removes a worker from client contact when needed.
Completes the screening, reports symptoms and exposures, and stays home when ill.

documentation: Basic health screening and TB screening result in the personnel file
Written clearance for any positive TB result
Annual health review and TB symptom questionnaire records
Re-screening tracking log
Hepatitis B vaccination offer, acceptance or declination
Exposure incident and post-exposure follow-up records
Quarterly compliance review

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: All employees, independent contractors and contractual employees who provide or supervise services, and all staff who maintain records
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] keeps complete, accurate, secure and retrievable records showing that every caregiver, nurse and contractor was screened, qualified and trained before being referred to a client, and that the agency can produce those records to OHCQ, MDH and other reviewers on request.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a record for every employee, independent contractor and contractual employee. Under COMAR 10.07.05.10, records of every pre-referral screening element are kept in the agency's business office at [ADDRESS]. Training records are kept in the individual's personnel file. Copies of current licenses, certifications and credentials are kept so they can be produced immediately on request. The agency keeps proof of workers' compensation coverage. Documentation of Medicaid service (dates and hours) is retained for 6 years from the date of service, as COMAR 10.09.84.05 requires. No one may be referred to a client until the screening record is complete. Personnel records are confidential and are released only to authorized persons.

definitions.definition: The documents showing completion of pre-referral screening: criminal history check, license or certification verification, basic health screening including TB, references, employment history, I-9 and identity and employment eligibility, in-person interview, and skills assessment and demonstration.
The individual file for each worker. It holds the application, job description, training records, evaluations, supervisory documentation, and corrective action.
A person supplied to the agency under a contract with another agency or entity, whose qualifications the contracting agency must be able to document.
The agency's licensed office location where screening records must be kept and be accessible to surveyors.

procedures: The Administrator designates a Personnel Records Custodian, [CUSTODIAN NAME], who is responsible for creating, maintaining, securing and auditing personnel and screening records.
Before any offer is finalized, the Custodian opens a personnel file and a screening record for the individual, using the agency's Personnel File Checklist.

The Custodian files the screening record in the business office. It contains the application, employment history, reference checks, the in-person interview record, the I-9 and identity documents, the criminal history check result, license or certification verification, the basic health screening with TB result, and the skills assessment and demonstration signed by the RN.

The Custodian places a copy of the current license or certification (RN, LPN, CNA, CMT) in the file and records the verification source, the date verified, the expiration date and the next verification due date (see PER-01).
The Custodian confirms that the criminal history check result is in the file and was cleared before the worker's first client assignment, including for nurses (see PER-02).
The Custodian obtains and files the written verification of worker qualifications needed for Medicaid personal assistance participation under COMAR 10.09.84.05.

The Custodian files the signed job description, the orientation record, the competency evaluation, CPR certification, and every annual or in-service training record in the personnel file with date, topic, trainer and hours (see PER-03). Any outside trainer's OHCQ written approval is kept with the training records.

For each contractor or contractual employee, the Custodian obtains from the subcontracting agency written evidence that it verified personnel information, and files that evidence in the business office (see GOV-09).

The Custodian maintains a Credential Tracking Log of all license, certification, CPR and TB or health screening expiration dates. The Log is reviewed monthly, and the Custodian notifies the worker and the Administrator 60 days and 30 days before an expiration.
A worker whose license, certification or required screening has lapsed is not scheduled until the Custodian documents renewal. The scheduler is notified the same day.
The Custodian keeps current workers' compensation insurance proof (certificate or policy declaration) in the business office, updates it at each renewal, and gives a copy to the Administrator.

Personnel files and screening records are stored in locked cabinets or in an access-controlled electronic system. Only the Administrator, the Director of Nursing, the Custodian and designated HR staff may access them. Health information and criminal history results are kept confidential and are not shared with clients.

Records are kept ready to produce immediately on request by OHCQ, MDH, OLTSS, DPICC or other authorized reviewers (see REC-03). The Custodian keeps an index of where each worker's records are located.
Service documentation supporting Medicaid claims, including EVV records, monthly signature verifications and visit notes, is retained for 6 years from the date of service (see REC-01 and SVC-09).

Personnel and screening records of separated workers are retained for at least 6 years after separation, so they remain available for the full Medicaid look-back and audit period, or for any longer period counsel advises. Records are destroyed only by shredding or secure deletion after the Administrator approves and a destruction log is signed.

Every quarter, the Custodian audits a sample of at least [NUMBER] files, or all files if there are fewer, against the checklist. Deficiencies are corrected within 10 business days and the results are reported to the QA committee (see GOV-04).

policies.title: Wage, Hour, Overtime and Leave Compliance
policies.applies_to: All employees, with Administrator, payroll, scheduling and HR staff responsible for compliance
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] pays caregivers and other employees lawfully under Maryland and federal wage and hour law, provides earned sick and safe leave, maintains workers' compensation coverage and fulfills wage reporting duties.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] pays every employee at or above the highest applicable minimum wage, pays overtime for hours over 40 in a workweek, and provides earned sick and safe leave as Maryland law requires. The agency maintains workers' compensation coverage at all times. It classifies aides as W-2 employees unless counsel advises otherwise in writing. Applicable minimum wage floors: State $15.00 per hour; Howard County $16.00; and, from July 1, 2026, Montgomery County $16.50 for home care employers with 11 or more employees that receive at least 75% of gross revenue from Medicaid, and otherwise $18.00 (51 or more employees), $16.50 (11 to 50 employees) or $15.95 (10 or fewer employees). Wage rates are re-checked every July 1 and whenever a county or State change is announced.

definitions.definition: A fixed, recurring period of seven consecutive 24-hour periods set by the agency as [WORKWEEK DEFINITION], used to calculate overtime.
All time an employee is required or permitted to work, including compensable travel between clients where required by law.
Leave under the Maryland Healthy Working Families Act, accruing at 1 hour per 30 hours worked with a 40-hour annual accrual, and paid for employers with 15 or more employees.
Maryland's Family and Medical Leave Insurance program, with employer and employee contributions beginning January 1, 2027 at a 0.9% total rate.
A federal FLSA exemption whose availability to third-party employers is governed by 29 CFR 552 and must be checked for its current status.

procedures: The Administrator designates a Payroll and Wage Compliance Lead, [PAYROLL LEAD NAME], who is responsible for the steps in this policy.

Each year by June 15 and again whenever a rate change is announced, the Lead reviews the State minimum wage ($15.00) and the county rates for each county where employees work, including Howard County ($16.00) and Montgomery County (rates effective July 1, 2026). Montgomery County status is determined by the agency's employee count and the share of gross revenue from Medicaid.

The Lead documents the determination of which Montgomery County tier applies to the agency, with the employee count, the Medicaid revenue percentage and the date calculated, and has the Administrator sign it. Rates are adjusted in the payroll system by the effective date, and the Lead keeps a rate-review memo in the compliance file.

Hourly rates for each worker are set at or above the highest minimum that applies to where the work is performed. The Lead checks the payroll system quarterly for any worker paid below the applicable rate.

Employees are paid for all hours worked. Hours are taken from verified EVV/ISAS records and approved timesheets for non-visit time such as orientation, training, supervisory visits and required meetings (see SVC-08).

Overtime is paid at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. Before any exemption is used, the Lead confirms the current federal status of the companionship exemption under 29 CFR 552 with counsel and documents the conclusion. Absent written counsel advice, aides are treated as non-exempt and receive overtime.
Schedulers may not assign hours that cause unapproved overtime. Projected overtime is flagged to the Administrator before the shift, and the scheduler records the approval (see SVC-07).

Travel time between clients during a workday is counted as hours worked and paid where required by law. The Lead sets and documents the method used, and aides record start and end times for travel on the timesheet.

Earned sick and safe leave accrues at 1 hour for every 30 hours worked, with a 40-hour annual accrual. Leave is paid if the agency has 15 or more employees. Before finalizing the leave policy, the Lead confirms any statutory caps and carryover with the Maryland Department of Labor and documents the answer.

The Lead tracks leave accrual and use in the payroll system and gives each employee a leave balance statement on request and at least quarterly. Leave may be used for the purposes the law allows, and no employee is penalized or retaliated against for using leave.

The Administrator keeps workers' compensation coverage in force for all employees. The Lead files the certificate in the business office (see PER-05) and the Administrator confirms renewal 30 days before expiration.

Employees injured at work report the injury to their supervisor the same day. The Director of Nursing or Administrator completes an injury report and the Lead files the claim with the carrier according to the carrier's requirements.

By October 1, 2026, the Lead plans for FAMLI by confirming payroll system settings, the employer and employee contribution split, and employee notices for contributions starting January 1, 2027 at a 0.9% total rate, and documents the plan.
Aides are classified as W-2 employees. A change of classification to independent contractor requires written advice of counsel and Administrator approval (see PER-08).

The Lead files the annual personal care aide wage report with the Department of Labor by September 1 (see PER-08) and tracks direct-care compensation against rates paid, in line with the Medicaid payment adequacy and rate transparency rule (42 CFR 441.302(k); 42 CFR 447.203). MDH has reported that the 80% direct-care compensation standard applies from July 9, 2030.

Any employee may raise a wage or leave concern with the Lead or the Administrator without retaliation. The Lead investigates within 5 business days, corrects any underpayment on the next payroll, and records the outcome.
The Lead reports payroll compliance findings, corrections and wage-rate reviews to the QA committee at least annually (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves wage determinations, maintains workers' compensation coverage, and ensures wage reports are filed.
Reviews wage floors, runs payroll, tracks overtime and leave, files required wage reports, and keeps compliance memos.
Avoids unapproved overtime, records travel time, and flags schedule changes to the Lead.
Ensures supervisory visits and training time are recorded and paid.
Record time accurately, report injuries at once, and raise pay concerns.
